query: What changes are reshaping the Industrial manufacturing industry, and what should companies focus on to support digital and green transformation?
draft_answer: Industrial manufacturing is being reshaped by digital transformation, especially through digital economy innovations, Industry 4.0, cloud computing, IoT, big data, AI, and related digital technologies that are changing production methods, management models, and innovation capability [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4319599463||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4313238684||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the papers, digitalization is repeatedly linked to sustainability outcomes, including greener technology systems, sustainable performance, and stronger corporate sustainability, but it is also clear that digitalization does not automatically produce sustainability benefits [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4360777148||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4302303968||ABSTRACT||000]. A common recommendation is to integrate digitalization with green technologies inside business processes, products, and models rather than treating them separately [https://openalex.org/W3182760100||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4313238684||ABSTRACT||001]. Companies should also focus on the practical enablers of transformation, including digital infrastructure, access to modern manufacturing technologies, and coordinated use of multiple digital transformation types such as service, model, organization, and process digitalization [https://openalex.org/W4360777148||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3164306258||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4313238684||ABSTRACT||001]. Several summaries emphasize that digital transformation can improve efficiency, supply-chain coordination, demand prediction, energy conservation, and environmental conservation, while also lowering costs and increasing productivity and innovation [https://openalex.org/W4319599463||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4309609041||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, firms face barriers such as integration challenges, economic and regulatory constraints, talent barriers, management costs, and uneven access to infrastructure [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4309609041||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3164306258||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence also suggests that transformation strategies should be sensitive to regional differences, because the digital economy’s effect on industrial green transformation varies across places and over time [https://openalex.org/W4387972406||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, companies are advised to strengthen green-tech innovation and environmental awareness, build the right infrastructure, and pursue collaborative, policy-supported digital-green integration to make transformation effective [https://openalex.org/W4387972406||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001].

Operational priorities include digital infrastructure, modern manufacturing technologies, and coordinated transformation across multiple digital domains, because these support efficiency, innovation, and sustainable performance [https://openalex.org/W4360777148||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3164306258||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4313238684||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence repeatedly notes implementation challenges, but it does not provide a single tested solution that works across all manufacturing contexts [https://openalex.org/W4302303968||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001].

query: Why nano-enhancers better for workpiece burn?

The same paper also notes that nano-enhancers with high hardness and spherical characteristics are better choices, implying that these properties further help address surface burn issues [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. A related review adds that nano-enhanced biolubricants benefit MQL machining through advanced lubrication and heat-transfer mechanisms, as well as distinctive film formation, atomization, and infiltration behaviors that improve workpiece performance [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. Across these sources, the common explanation is that nano-enhancers outperform conventional fluids because they can manage heat and friction more effectively while forming more functional lubricant films [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. However, several provided summaries do not actually discuss workpiece burn or nano-enhancers, so the evidence base is limited and not fully direct for every context [https://openalex.org/W4207036872||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4322505914||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4324057306||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do carbon dots compare with inorganic quantum dots as optical nanomaterials, and what sustainability issues are highlighted in the review?
draft_answer: Across these reviews, carbon dots/carbon quantum dots are consistently portrayed as promising optical nanomaterials with attractive properties such as tunable fluorescence or luminescence, biocompatibility, low toxicity, and applications in bioimaging, sensing, optoelectronics, photocatalysis, and environmental monitoring [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4406866034||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4313550231||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers explicitly frame them as a functional and sustainable alternative to incumbent optical nanomaterials, especially inorganic quantum dots, noting advantages such as biomass-based synthesis and freedom from toxic or precious metals and critical raw materials [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the reviews do not provide a detailed side-by-side optical performance comparison with inorganic quantum dots; instead, they mainly position carbon dots as replacement candidates based on sustainability, cost, and biocompatibility rather than direct quantitative benchmarking [https://openalex.org/W4318483232||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000]. Sustainability concerns recur throughout the literature and include the environmental burden of synthesis solvents, energy use, material inefficiency, safety, and waste management, with some methods described as wasteful because they rely on non-sustainable solvents and energy [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000]. In response, the reviews emphasize green chemistry, Safe and Sustainable by Design approaches, standardization, improved purification, and renewable or waste-derived precursors such as biomass, food waste, plastics, and other natural sources [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4406866034||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4313550231||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4387573993||ABSTRACT||000]. Several reviews also identify practical limitations that constrain wider adoption, including low quantum yield, reproducibility problems, heterogeneity, scalability challenges, and the need for more precise control over properties [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports carbon dots as a greener, lower-toxicity class of optical nanomaterials with broad application potential, while also showing that sustainability is not automatic and depends on cleaner synthesis, better efficiency, and more transparent reporting of inputs and outputs [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Carbon dots are repeatedly described as promising optical nanomaterials because of tunable fluorescence/luminescence, low toxicity, biocompatibility, and applications in imaging, sensing, optoelectronics, photocatalysis, and environmental monitoring [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4406866034||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4313550231||ABSTRACT||000].

Some reviews present carbon dots as sustainable alternatives to inorganic quantum dots, emphasizing biomass-derived synthesis and the absence of toxic or precious metals and critical raw materials [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000].

The reviews do not provide a strong direct side-by-side optical comparison with inorganic quantum dots; instead, they mostly position carbon dots as replacement candidates on the basis of sustainability, cost, and biocompatibility [https://openalex.org/W4318483232||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000].

Sustainability issues highlighted for carbon-dot synthesis include solvent choice, energy and material efficiency, safety, waste management, and the need to avoid wasteful non-sustainable methods [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000].

The reviews call for green chemistry, Safe and Sustainable by Design approaches, standardization, improved purification, and quantitative reporting of solvents, consumables, energy, starting materials, and byproducts [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The provided summaries rarely include direct head-to-head comparisons with inorganic quantum dots, so the evidence is stronger for sustainability-oriented positioning than for optical performance benchmarking.

Several reviews are based on broad survey-style claims rather than quantitative synthesis, and the summaries note unresolved issues such as low quantum yield, reproducibility, heterogeneity, and scalability.

query: How FT's do they add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when they fulfill their boundary-spanning role?
draft_answer: Across the papers, the strongest direct evidence indicates that FTs do add their own interpretation when performing boundary-spanning work on sustainability requirements, rather than applying rules mechanically [https://openalex.org/W3205987731||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4410729659||ABSTRACT||001]. One study explicitly says FTs add personal interpretation and that their boundary-spanning actions can be compliance-oriented or improvement-oriented, showing that interpretation can change both the meaning and the direction of the action taken [https://openalex.org/W3205987731||ABSTRACT||001]. A related paper on sustainability standard-setting describes the arena as highly contested and says actors negotiate interoperability, materiality, and connectivity, implying that interpretation is strategic and shaped by competing priorities [https://openalex.org/W4410729659||ABSTRACT||001]. Another paper on sustainability reporting regulation similarly finds that harmonization is still far from achieved because actors have diverse objectives and cannot renounce their particular perspectives, which supports the idea that boundary-spanning actors bring their own perspectives to requirements [https://openalex.org/W4225388860||ABSTRACT||001]. The broader literature also aligns with this pattern by showing that sustainability materiality is ambiguous and contested, and that professionals’ subjective understandings and contextual circumstances shape how sustainability is operationalized [https://openalex.org/W4289767614||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4313908265||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, some papers only address sustainability models or reporting frameworks at a general level and do not directly study FT behavior, so they support interpretation as a general phenomenon rather than providing direct evidence about FTs specifically [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4382811259||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4313644972||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the synthesis suggests that FT boundary-spanning is not neutral rule transmission but a socially and contextually influenced interpretive role, with evidence pointing to both compliance and improvement orientations and to negotiation of contested sustainability meanings [https://openalex.org/W3205987731||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4410729659||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4313908265||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How mask mandates help Covid-19 cases, and what did the study find?
draft_answer: Across the supplied studies, the strongest direct evidence on mask mandates and COVID-19 case counts comes from a U.S. state-level analysis that estimated mask mandates and compliance while controlling for mobility [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. That study found that higher mobility increased case growth, and that a mask mandate could offset about one third of that mobility-related increase in the most conservative estimates [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. It also reported that mask mandates were more effective in states with higher compliance, and that a national mask mandate on May 15, 2020 could have reduced total U.S. infections by 23.7% to 30.4% by November 15, 2020 [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate study found that longer-lasting COVID-19 prevention measures, including face mask mandates, were associated with lower incidence than having the policy in place for less than one month, with the largest reductions seen in socially vulnerable communities [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. This same study reported that for face mask mandates, the difference in marginal mean monthly incidence ranged from -4 cases per 100,000 in low-SVI counties to -401 cases per 100,000 in high-SVI counties [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. Other papers in the set support the general protective role of masks, but they focus on PPE rather than mandates: a rapid review found face masks significantly protected healthcare workers from infection and concluded that PPE, especially N95 masks, reduces risk [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||001], and another study concluded that surgical masks provided better protection than cloth masks among healthcare workers [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001]. One broader non-pharmaceutical-interventions paper also suggests that measures within a larger containment strategy helped achieve rapid and sustained containment of COVID-19, though it does not specifically isolate mask mandates [https://openalex.org/W3215618709||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence in these summaries suggests mask mandates help reduce COVID-19 cases, especially when compliance is higher and mandates are sustained longer, but the exact estimates come from observational analyses and may vary by setting [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: A U.S. state-level study found that mask mandates could offset about one third of the case-growth increase associated with higher mobility, and that a national mandate on May 15, 2020 could have reduced total U.S. infections by 23.7% to 30.4% by November 15, 2020 [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000].
Mask mandates were more effective in states with higher compliance [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000].

Longer durations of prevention measures, including face mask mandates, were associated with lower COVID-19 incidence than short durations, with larger reductions in high-social-vulnerability counties [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001].

A rapid review and meta-analysis found that face masks significantly protected healthcare workers from COVID-19 infection, and concluded that PPE, especially N95 masks, helps reduce infection risk [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||001].
Among healthcare workers, surgical masks provided better protection than cloth masks, while the benefit of powered air-purifying respirators was less clear [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several cited findings are observational or model-based, so they show association or estimated counterfactual effects rather than definitive causal proof [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001].

Some papers in the set do not address mask mandates at all and instead focus on PPE for healthcare workers, ventilation, stigma, recruitment models, or broader non-pharmaceutical interventions, which limits how directly they answer the mandate question [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001][pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3215618709||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9805824||ABSTRACT||001][pmc_PMC10008035||ABSTRACT||001].

The magnitude of benefit appears to vary by compliance, duration of policy, and community social vulnerability, so the effect of mandates is not uniform across settings [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001].

The evidence summarized here does not provide randomized trials of mask mandates or a single unified estimate of their effect across all populations and time periods [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What role did hexagonal boron nitride play in the study of canola oil as a bio-lubricant, and what details are provided about its evaluation?
draft_answer: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) appears in the evidence as a solid nano-additive used in canola oil to improve tribological performance, addressing the fact that canola oil alone was described as weaker than petroleum-based oils [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. In that study, hBN was tested in canola oil at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 wt.% [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. Its evaluation relied on dynamic viscosity measurements and pin-on-disk testing in the boundary lubrication regime, with coefficient of friction and wear as the main outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. The best result for hBN alone was at 1.0 wt.%, which produced the lowest coefficient of friction and was reported as 40% lower than the base oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. The study also combined hBN with graphene nanoplatelet in mixed formulations, and these blends achieved 56% friction reduction and 90% wear reduction versus base oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. Across the broader literature, hBN is also discussed as a tribologically functional additive in sustainable biolubricant formulations, but the other supplied papers do not provide canola-oil-specific evaluation details [https://openalex.org/W4390658388||ABSTRACT||000]. More generally, the reviews agree that plant-based or bio-based lubricants are renewable and biodegradable, while also noting that performance is often improved by adding nanomaterials [https://openalex.org/W4401870224||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390658388||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does organizational learning capability contribute to radical innovation?
draft_answer: The strongest direct evidence suggests that organizational learning capability contributes to radical innovation by acting as an enabling organizational context rather than as a standalone output [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000]. In one study, organizational learning capability fully mediated the relationship between stewardship leader behavior and radical innovation, indicating that leadership influences radical innovation through learning processes [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000]. The same evidence specifies that this capability supports experimentation, dialog, participative decision-making, risk-taking, and interaction with the external environment, all of which are presented as conditions that foster radical innovation [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000]. By contrast, a heavily calcified-lesion registry showed that calcification mainly increased procedural complexity, but orbital atherectomy still achieved high procedural success and no primary safety events within 30 days, suggesting that complication risk depends on the clinical context and treatment strategy [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||001]. The review also notes that for similar CAC levels, absolute ASCVD risk can differ by region and ethnicity, indicating that the complication risk associated with CAC may vary across populations [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000]. However, some papers in the set do not address coronary calcification at all, so the evidence is incomplete for defining a universal complication profile [pmc_PMC10140970||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10141707||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9806495||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do PAs create public value in sustainability reporting?

More broadly, sustainability reporting is presented as a structured, theory-of-change-driven practice that uses reporting standards and frameworks to support continuous improvement and alignment with international standards [https://openalex.org/W4406062330||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402984150||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence is not fully consistent on the role of public administrations in every context: one paper explicitly says public value is created through reporting’s effects on multiple stakeholder groups but does not specify PAs’ exact role [https://openalex.org/W4390267129||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: In the public-sector literature, PAs create public value through sustainability reporting by preserving and disseminating public value, obtaining legitimacy and stakeholder support, and building operational capacity [https://openalex.org/W4320719832||ABSTRACT||000].

PAs can also create public value by designing reporting forms that hybridize integrated reporting and the SDGs to support sustainability delivery in practice [https://openalex.org/W3121263816||ABSTRACT||000].

Sustainability reporting creates public value by increasing transparency and accountability to stakeholders and by clarifying economic, social, and environmental impacts [https://openalex.org/W4402984150||ABSTRACT||000].

One chapter argues that public value in sustainability reporting is created primarily through stakeholder accountability in materiality determination, rather than through valuation or stewardship roles [https://openalex.org/W4289767614||ABSTRACT||000].

The public-sector sustainability reporting field is still at an early stage, with research showing an unsteady but slightly upward trend and a need to incorporate mandatory non-financial reporting regulation [https://openalex.org/W3147261195||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries are conceptual, bibliometric, or literature-based rather than based on direct causal tests, so the mechanisms of public value creation are often proposed rather than demonstrated [https://openalex.org/W4406062330||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3147261195||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence is context-specific, with findings drawn from particular settings such as Italian Port Authorities, the Emilia-Romagna Region, GCC, and Indonesia, which limits generalizability [https://openalex.org/W4320719832||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3121263816||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||002] [https://openalex.org/W4313418383||ABSTRACT||001].

Materiality and reporting quality are described as ambiguous or uneven, and some studies note shallow diffusion or less acceptable reliability, indicating that public value depends on implementation quality [https://openalex.org/W4289767614||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4313418383||ABSTRACT||001].

One summary notes that public value is created through effects on multiple stakeholder groups but does not specify the exact role of PAs, leaving their contribution partly unclear in that literature [https://openalex.org/W4390267129||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do sustainable technologies and environmantal management relate in the context of Industry 4.0 and SDGs, and what did the study find about enterprises preference for environmental aspects in business management?
draft_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies and environmental management are presented as closely linked through Industry 4.0’s potential to improve environmental sustainability, especially in manufacturing and logistics [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001]. Several studies argue that Industry 4.0 technologies can improve understanding of production and supply chains, increase manufacturing efficiency, and reduce resource consumption, thereby supporting environmental sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers extend this connection to SDGs, stating that the convergence of Industry 4.0 with the SDGs improves environmental sustainability and environmental performance and can create ecological support [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also frames sustainable technologies such as clean energy, green logistics, reverse logistics, and renewable energy as enablers of industrial development and growth when combined with Industry 4.0 innovations under the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one study cautions that some Industry 4.0-related technologies can have negative environmental effects, including air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive use of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the literature review papers suggest broad agreement that Industry 4.0 can support environmental management, but also note that the relationship has been fragmented and not fully clarified in the literature [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000]. In terms of enterprises’ preferences, the Slovak enterprise study found that more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management and that more than 82% implemented the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That same study reported a significant relationship between environmental management in the context of SDGs and sustainability in production and logistics, including a significant relationship with renewable energy technology use in industry [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Industry 4.0 technologies are repeatedly described as supporting environmental sustainability by improving manufacturing efficiency, understanding supply chains, and reducing resource consumption [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000].

The convergence of Industry 4.0 and the SDGs is presented as improving environmental sustainability and environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

Sustainable technologies such as clean energy, green/reverse logistics, and renewable energy are described as creating conditions for industrial development and future growth when combined with Industry 4.0 innovations under the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

One study found that more than 70% of 105 Slovak enterprises preferred environmental aspects in business management, and more than 82% implemented the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

The Slovak study also found a significant relationship between enterprise environmental management in the context of SDGs and sustainability in production and logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

A review of the literature notes that the Industry 4.0–sustainability relationship is still unclear and fragmented, even though Industry 4.0 is widely discussed as relevant to sustainability practices and performance [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers are literature reviews or conceptual studies, so many conclusions are based on synthesized prior research rather than direct causal tests [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000].

The strongest enterprise-level evidence comes from a single study of 105 Slovak enterprises, which limits how broadly the preference for environmental aspects can be generalized [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

Some studies emphasize benefits, but at least one also reports possible negative environmental effects from Industry 4.0-related technologies, showing that the relationship is not uniformly positive [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000].

Not all studies directly address the enterprise preference question, and several abstracts explicitly do not provide that result [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120619572||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do energy resourses and renewable energy in mining together help with environmental sustainability and sustainable development, and what good effects are said about using renewable energy in mining for sustainability?
draft_answer: Across the papers, the main idea is that mining sustainability improves when energy use is reduced and cleaner energy sources are adopted, because mining is energy-intensive and often reliant on fossil fuels [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||001]. One paper argues that sustainable mining should minimize resource and energy consumption, waste, and other environmental harms such as dust pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and acid mine drainage across all stages of mining [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||001]. Another study reports that green mining technologies, including electric vehicles and renewable energy sources, decrease carbon emissions and lower energy use while improving waste management compared with traditional methods [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000]. In addition, renewable energy in mining is said to support Sustainable Development Goals by creating jobs, reducing environmental pollution, increasing knowledge in mining areas, promoting a circular economy, and lowering operating costs [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the literature warns that renewable energy should not be judged only by carbon reduction, because hidden impacts in energy-generation processes can create broader sustainability tradeoffs and can either enable or inhibit progress toward the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000]. This broader view is consistent with MASI’s emphasis on assessing mining sustainability across environmental, social, and economic dimensions to support ecological preservation, social welfare, and economic viability [https://openalex.org/W4393928445||ABSTRACT||001]. Evidence from sustainability reporting also suggests that these benefits are not automatic, since many companies still showed increased air emissions, water use, and energy usage, with no improvement in renewable energy utilization or waste recycling [https://openalex.org/W3165375152||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that combining energy-resource management with renewable energy can help environmental sustainability and sustainable development in mining, but only when supported by planning, regulation, and attention to wider social and economic effects [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Mining sustainability is linked to reducing energy consumption and other environmental burdens across the mining lifecycle [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||001].

Integrating renewable energy in mining is reported to reduce carbon emissions, lower energy use, and improve waste management relative to traditional methods [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000].

Renewable energy in mining is said to support sustainable development through job creation, pollution reduction, more knowledge, circular economy effects, and lower operating costs [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001].

Renewable energy systems can also have hidden sustainability impacts, so they must be evaluated beyond carbon emissions alone and in relation to the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000].

Sustainability reporting found increased air emissions, water use, and energy usage for most companies, with no improvement in renewable energy utilization or waste recycling [https://openalex.org/W3165375152||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries note missing or limited evidence on renewable energy in mining, including papers that do not address the topic directly [https://openalex.org/W4393928445||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3175891888||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3194681237||ABSTRACT||000].

The reported benefits of renewable energy in mining are not universal, since one study found increased air emissions, water use, and energy usage for most companies and no improvement in renewable energy utilization [https://openalex.org/W3165375152||ABSTRACT||000].

One paper warns that renewable energy can create sustainability tradeoffs if hidden impacts in energy generation are ignored, so environmental gains may not fully translate into broader sustainable development benefits [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence mentions challenges such as lack of information, high investment, lack of skilled labor, and high maintenance costs, suggesting implementation barriers remain [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How the sustainability assessment and evaluation frameworks in the district heating and PT evaluation studies are linked, and which method was most used, plus how do they relate to CO2 emissions reduction in the urban transport example?
draft_answer: Across the district heating, Positive Energy Districts (PEDs), and public transport (PT) studies, sustainability assessment and evaluation are linked by a common use of indicators or KPIs to compare alternatives and support decision-making, but the emphasis differs by domain [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000]. In district heating and related energy-system work, the assessment framework is organized around multi-dimensional indicator sets, such as social, economic, environmental, technical, and institutional dimensions, while other studies broaden this further to include technological, political, and institutional indicators [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The PED review similarly relies on KPIs, European standards/initiatives, Sustainable Development Agenda indicators, and literature-based metrics, but stresses that the KPI framework still needs better integration and harmonization with Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000]. For PT, the dominant evaluation frameworks are Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM), followed by Assessment Indicator Models (AIM), and among MCDM methods the Analytical Hierarchy Process was the most frequently used approach [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]. That means the most-used method explicitly identified in the PT evidence is AHP, while in the PED evidence LCA is highlighted as the most used method, showing that “most used” depends on the study domain and review scope rather than a single universal method [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000]. In the district heating study using MCDA, several methods were compared, including WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, and sensitivity analysis was used to judge which approach was most credible [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The urban sustainability/project-evaluation papers reinforce the same general logic that indicators are used to measure progress, performance, and weaknesses over time, but they do not provide a direct district-heating-to-PT linkage or a specific urban transport case study beyond the indicator framing [https://openalex.org/W4377861392||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3162569529||ABSTRACT||001]. On CO2 emissions reduction, the clearest link appears in the renewable-energy/district-heating evaluation framework, where CO2 emission and GHG emission reduction are explicitly listed as environmental indicators [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001]. So, the shared thread is an indicator-based sustainability evaluation logic, with MCDM/AHP dominant in PT and LCA prominent in PEDs, while CO2 reduction is treated as a measured environmental outcome in the urban transport/energy-evaluation framing rather than as a standalone result across all studies [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: District heating and related energy-system studies use multi-dimensional indicator frameworks to connect sustainability assessment with evaluation, including social, economic, environmental, technical, and institutional dimensions [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

In the PT review, the preferred evaluation framework is Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM), followed by Assessment Indicator Models (AIM), and the most frequently used MCDM method is the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001].

The PED review says sustainability assessment relies on KPIs, standards, Sustainable Development Agenda indicators, and literature-based metrics, and it calls for better integration and harmonization with Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000].

In the district heating MCDA study, WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA were all applied, and sensitivity analysis was used to assess credibility and interpret differences among methods [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

The clearest CO2-emissions linkage appears in the renewable-energy/district-heating evaluation framework, where CO2 emission and GHG emission reduction are explicitly listed as environmental indicators [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The papers do not establish a single unified framework across district heating, PEDs, and PT; instead, they use related but different indicator sets and methods, so cross-domain linkage is partial [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence is inconsistent on the "most used" method because PT highlights AHP, while PED highlights LCA, and district heating MCDA compares multiple methods without naming one universal winner [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

No provided chunk gives a direct urban transport case study demonstrating CO2 emissions reduction outcomes, so the transport link to CO2 can only be stated as an indicator-based framing rather than a verified empirical result [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3162569529||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do innovation, CEOs' sustainability orientation, and green governance relate to sustainability and environmental performance in firms?
draft_answer: Across the summaries, innovation appears to be consistently associated with better sustainability-related outcomes, but the strength and pathway of that relationship varies by context and outcome. Green innovation is reported to have a significant positive relationship with environmental sustainability in industrial firms, and this link is mediated by innovation climate, with green motivational strategies and green abilities strengthening the effect of innovation practices [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||001]. In another study, green innovation capabilities indirectly influence the effect of social and economic sustainability on firm performance, although they do not indirectly affect the relationship between environmental sustainability and firm performance [https://openalex.org/W3200508375||ABSTRACT||001]. Sustainability-oriented innovations also show a strong positive impact on firms’ economic performance, with green competitive advantage and green image serving as mediators, and green organizational identity further supporting green image through green commitment [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000]. On the leadership side, the evidence points to environmentally aware leadership as beneficial: green transformational leadership is positively related to green performance, and this relationship is mediated by green organizational culture and green engagement [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000]. For CEOs specifically, the available evidence does not directly test CEOs’ sustainability orientation, so no firm conclusion can be drawn about that variable from these summaries alone [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]. Green governance also appears important, but in a configurational rather than universal way: corporate governance bundles involving CEO power, board capital, and ownership structure generate multiple sufficient paths to high environmental innovation, and both powerful and weak CEOs can facilitate environmental innovation when paired with suitable governance arrangements [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, a genuinely implemented sustainable strategy improves firm performance and favorable environmental results, yet its effectiveness depends on ownership dispersion and board independence, and sector-specific differences mean there is no single governance formula that works across all industries [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that innovation, leadership orientation, and governance design can support sustainability and environmental performance, but they also suggest that these effects are often indirect, mediated, and contingent on internal organizational and governance conditions [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Green innovation has a significant positive relationship with environmental sustainability in industrial firms, and innovation climate mediates this link [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||001]

Green innovation capabilities indirectly affect the relationship between social and economic sustainability and firm performance, but not the relationship between environmental sustainability and firm performance [https://openalex.org/W3200508375||ABSTRACT||001]
Sustainability-oriented innovations improve firms’ economic performance, with green competitive advantage and green image acting as mediators [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000]

Green transformational leadership is positively related to green performance, and green organizational culture and green engagement mediate this relationship [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000]

Corporate governance bundles involving CEO power, board capital, and ownership structure can produce multiple sufficient paths to high environmental innovation, showing that governance design matters [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]

A genuinely implemented sustainable strategy improves firm performance and favorable environmental results, but its effectiveness depends on ownership structure and board independence [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000]

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries explicitly do not provide direct evidence on CEOs’ sustainability orientation, so that part of the query cannot be answered conclusively from the available papers [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000].

The governance findings are highly contingent and configurational, meaning there is no single universal governance model for sustainability or environmental performance across firms or industries [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000].

Some evidence is sector-specific, focusing on manufacturing, industrial firms, Chinese SMEs, or dirty firms, which limits how broadly the results can be generalized [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4381617377||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000].

At least one summary notes a broader research gap on how corporate governance actors interact to shape environmental sustainability outcomes, indicating that the literature remains incomplete [https://openalex.org/W3132785017||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do the themes of "energy resources," "clean and distributed energy," and "energy transitions" connect across the context in explaining both environmental sustainability and workforce implications, and what does the context say about the role of clean energy, renewable electricity, and training in this transition?
draft_answer: Across the papers, “energy resources,” “clean and distributed energy,” and “energy transitions” are connected as parts of a broader shift from conventional energy systems toward more sustainable, lower-carbon systems that must satisfy environmental, economic, social, and institutional goals [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3154213043||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries emphasize that this transition is not only about emissions reduction but also about environmental sustainability, policy coherence, and broader development goals such as green growth, social inclusion, and climate protection [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001]. The context also treats energy resources as unevenly distributed and the transition as technically and economically constrained, noting the need for renewable adoption, storage, resilient grids, and a sustainable mix of renewable and limited nonrenewable sources to maintain stability and flexibility [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4387418575||ABSTRACT||000]. Clean and distributed energy appears especially as part of a democratic, inclusive, and stakeholder-sensitive transition, where perceptions of centralized versus distributed models, sustainability, and the speed of decarbonization matter for how quickly the transition can proceed [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000]. On the environmental side, renewable energy is repeatedly presented as helping combat climate change and advance sustainable development, while also being linked to resource conservation, environmental protection, and climate change policy priorities [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001]. On the workforce side, the papers connect transition with job creation, economic growth, social equity, and green job formation, but also note uneven impacts across sectors and regions, implying that adaptation pressures will not be distributed evenly [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4387418575||ABSTRACT||000]. The context specifically says that renewable energy investment and workforce training should support green economic transformation, and another paper highlights human capital development as part of advancing the transition [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that clean energy and renewable electricity are central mechanisms in the transition, but the transition is framed as requiring policy support, infrastructure, stakeholder coordination, and skills development rather than technology alone [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: The papers frame energy transitions as multidimensional shifts that must balance environmental sustainability with economic, social, technical, and institutional considerations [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3154213043||ABSTRACT||000].

Renewable and clean energy are presented as key drivers of climate mitigation, sustainable development, and green economic growth [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001].

The transition has workforce implications, including job creation, green job growth, social equity concerns, and uneven sectoral adjustment pressures [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4387418575||ABSTRACT||000].

Several summaries explicitly say that workforce training, human capital development, or similar capacity-building measures are needed to advance the energy transition [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001].

Clean and distributed energy is discussed in connection with democratic, inclusive, and stakeholder-sensitive transition models, not just technical decarbonization [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries explicitly note that clean energy, renewable electricity, or training are not directly mentioned, so some links among the themes are inferred from broader transition language rather than stated verbatim [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3154213043||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence is geographically and contextually uneven, with some papers focused on specific settings such as Portugal, BRICS, or a Vision 2030 policy framework, which limits how universally the claims can be applied [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001].

The summaries describe broad themes but provide little direct empirical detail on how training is implemented, how renewable electricity specifically changes labor markets, or how tradeoffs are resolved in practice [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4387418575||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the themes of "Environmental sustainability", "Sustainability implementation barriers", and "Sustainable residential buildings" connect when comparing off-site construction research with the barrier analysis in Ghana and the "Mostadam" approach in Saudi Arabia, and what sustainability-related findings are highlighted across these contexts?
draft_answer: Across the supplied papers, the clearest common thread is that environmental sustainability is treated as a practical building and housing problem, not just an abstract goal: Ghanaian construction research evaluates sustainability across the full project life cycle using indicators such as water quality, air quality, energy use and conservation, and environmental compliance and management [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||001]. In the Ghana barrier studies, sustainability implementation is shown to be constrained by multiple barrier sets, including cultural, economic, technical knowledge, regulatory, management, standards, society, and knowledge barriers, with management-related barriers and economics/regulation often emerging as especially important [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132259306||ABSTRACT||000]. The Saudi Arabia Mostadam discussion connects most directly to sustainable residential buildings by presenting the rating system as a pathway toward sustainable development, practical strategies, future policy, and Vision 2030 city transformation [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. Read together, these papers suggest that sustainability in the built environment depends both on defining environmental performance goals and on overcoming implementation barriers that slow adoption in real projects [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001]. The residential-building literature reinforces this by showing that sustainability can also be linked to affordability and lifecycle economics, with design techniques, passive design, recycled and local materials, and socio-technical innovation improving both sustainability and cost outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001]. Similarly, prefabricated construction research in Southern Africa reports higher overall sustainability performance for innovative prefabricated methods, tying environmental sustainability to sustainable affordable housing and lifecycle energy and cost assessment [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000]. A broader pattern across contexts is that sustainability-related findings are framed as actionable guidance for policymakers, designers, and industry stakeholders, whether through barrier removal, better education and policy support, or design and rating-system strategies [https://openalex.org/W3145060410||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the evidence does not provide direct off-site construction results or a full side-by-side comparison between the specific Ghana, Saudi Arabia, and off-site construction contexts, so that linkage remains limited by the supplied summaries [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001].

query: In the context of Environmental sustainability reporting and Sustainability reporting, how do the Bahrain industrial companies" materiality matrices relate to improved environmental performance, and how does this compare with the UK evidence on whether reporting that follows guidelines and a business-case approach actually improves sustainability performance?

The same Bahrain study also says materiality matrices can improve report contents by incorporating stakeholders’ views, which in turn improves sustainability report quality and supports SDG implementation [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence on sufficiency transitions is vague: most papers mention sustainability, sufficiency, sustainable consumption, or pro-sustainable behaviour only in broad terms and do not specify concrete consumption changes [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000].

There is an unresolved tension between marketing for competitiveness/profit and marketing for ecological or social well-being, including the risk of greenwashing when firms adopt sustainability selectively [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000].

Some evidence is geographically or contextually limited, such as the SME findings about low awareness, high costs, and weak government support, which may not generalize broadly [https://openalex.org/W4323049305||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How sustainability reporting link with SDGs and sustainability performance, it matter from the supply chain framework too?
draft_answer:
Across the papers, sustainability reporting is generally treated as a way to connect corporate or supply-chain activities to the SDGs and to assess sustainability performance, but the strength of that connection varies by study [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies support a positive link: sustainability reporting can be monitored against the SDGs, and reporting score indices have been built to help investors and stakeholders measure sustainable performance and commitment to the global sustainability agenda [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001]. Relatedly, integrated reporting is framed as a corporate strategy for achieving SDGs and assessing SDG performance using common metrics, although the paper notes comparisons between companies remain difficult [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, evidence from a large study of 8,500 companies suggests that SDG reporting can be disconnected from actual sustainability performance and may involve arbitrary selection of goals rather than a grounded performance basis [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000]. This creates an important contradiction: some papers present reporting as a useful performance tool, while others show that current reporting practices may not reliably reflect real sustainability outcomes or progress across multiple SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000].

From a supply chain framework, the evidence is strong that sustainability matters beyond the firm boundary. One paper finds that sustainable supply chain practices have positive and significant relationships with both financial performance and the SDGs, and explicitly recommends implementing sustainability from supplier to customer to improve efficiency and reduce negative environmental and social impacts [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001]. Another study proposes a supply-chain sustainability assessment framework grounded in GRI that measures both a company’s and its suppliers’ sustainability performance, while improving communication of environmental and social progress to stakeholders [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. A further paper argues that SSCM, technology adoption, and performance measurement are important for sustainability and proposes frameworks for achieving SDGs through SSCM and deploying sustainability indicators [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000].

However, the literature also shows that supply-chain or life-cycle links to SDGs are not yet fully harmonized. One study notes that some indicators have no direct or indirect connection to any SDG because SDGs lack a life-cycle-thinking perspective and there is limited discussion of workers, consumers, and value-chain actors [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001]. Another review says SDGs and LCSA are complementary but there is still no generally agreed way to set up their connections, so further research is needed to consistently link metrics to SDG goals [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the best-supported conclusion is that sustainability reporting can matter for SDGs and sustainability performance, especially when it is tied to materiality, indicators, and supply-chain assessment rather than just symbolic disclosure [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Sustainability reporting is often presented as a tool for monitoring SDG alignment and measuring sustainable performance, but some studies find that reporting does not reliably reflect actual sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000]

Sustainable supply chain management is linked to both SDGs and financial performance, and one study recommends implementing sustainability across the supplier-to-customer chain [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001]

A supply-chain sustainability assessment framework based on GRI was designed to measure a company’s and suppliers’ sustainability performance and improve communication of environmental and social progress [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]

Some studies found no direct or indirect connection between certain indicators and SDGs, partly because SDGs lack a life-cycle-thinking perspective and because value-chain actors are under-discussed [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001]

SDGs and LCSA are described as complementary, but there is still no harmonized way to connect them, so more research is needed to link metrics consistently to SDG goals [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001]

Materiality-based reporting and sustainability indicators are presented as ways to improve report quality and better connect sustainability reporting to environmental performance measurement and SDG implementation [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000]

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers note that reporting practices can be disconnected from real sustainability performance, so the evidence supports a link in principle but not always in practice [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000].

The supply-chain and life-cycle literature still lacks a harmonized framework for linking indicators to SDGs, and some studies explicitly call for further research [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001].

Some papers do not address supply-chain frameworks directly, so conclusions about the supply chain dimension cannot be generalized from all reporting studies [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the circular economy and sustainable recycling approaches in textile waste and polymeric membranes reduce environmental impact?
draft_answer:
Across the papers, circular economy approaches are presented as a way to reduce environmental impact by keeping materials in use longer, lowering waste, and reducing demand for new resource extraction in both textiles and polymeric materials. In textile waste, reuse, repair, recycling, reduction, and related strategies are repeatedly described as mechanisms for cutting waste from fast-fashion production and consumption cycles, with repair extending garment life and reducing the need for new production [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001]. Several textile studies also argue that circular models can turn waste into valuable outputs such as recycled yarn, regenerated fibers, biofilms, biodegradable composites, and biofuels, while reducing water, resource, and energy consumption [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||002]. Another textile paper frames a closed-loop system in which post-consumer items are transformed into recycled fiber, explicitly aiming to reduce pollution and resource waste [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. The textile literature agrees that recycling is important but not sufficient on its own, because technological, awareness, investment, and policy barriers can limit effectiveness and existing waste-management programs have often been unsuccessful [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000].

For polymeric materials, the review emphasizes that persistent plastic waste makes traditional mechanical recycling insufficient, and it presents chemical and biological options such as pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation as more efficient and sustainable alternatives [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. These approaches are explicitly linked to closed-loop and circular plastic economy strategies, which are described as key steps toward reducing environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. The textile papers and the polymer review converge on the same general principle: sustainability improves when waste is treated as a resource and processes are designed for circularity rather than linear disposal [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the textile literature suggests that better environmental outcomes depend on designing materials and finishes for end-of-life recycling, and on supportive systems such as traceability and improved waste-management infrastructure [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports the view that circular economy and sustainable recycling reduce environmental impact by extending product life, increasing material recovery, and lowering pollution and resource use, but their success depends on overcoming technological and institutional barriers [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4283362208||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: In textiles, circular economy strategies such as reuse, repair, recycling, and reduction are used to cut waste and environmental impacts from fast-fashion production and consumption cycles [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000].

Repair and reuse can extend garment lifespan, reduce the need for new production, and lessen environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001].

Textile circular economy models can convert waste into secondary resources such as recycled yarn, regenerated fibers, biofilms, biodegradable composites, and biofuels while reducing water, resource, and energy consumption [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||002].

For polymeric materials, chemical and biological recycling methods including pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation are presented as more efficient and sustainable alternatives to traditional mechanical recycling [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000].
Closed-loop and circular economy strategies are described as key steps toward reducing environmental impact in plastic recycling [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000].

The literature also stresses that recycling effectiveness is limited by technological, awareness, investment, and policy barriers, so supportive systems are needed for circular approaches to work well [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The textile evidence is largely review-based and conceptual, so the summaries do not provide direct comparative measurements of how much environmental impact is reduced by each strategy.
The polymeric-membrane-related evidence is limited; one paper discusses polymer recycling broadly, but the provided summaries do not specify detailed membrane-specific mechanisms or outcomes.
Several textile sources note that recycling is constrained by technological, investment, awareness, and policy barriers, suggesting that benefits may not be fully realized in current practice.
Some evidence is truncated or general in scope, especially the paper mentioning biological approaches for textile waste, so mechanism-level conclusions remain limited.

query: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?
draft_answer: Across the papers, textile waste management is consistently framed as needing a shift away from dumping and toward circular, resource-recovery systems that support reuse, recycling, and closed-loop production [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies show that waste conversion can be used to transform textile waste into valuable outputs, including recycled fibers, separable fiber fractions, and even new products or clean energy through biotechnologies [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||001]. More specific conversion routes include chemical and biotechnological methods such as acid hydrolysis, enzymatic recycling, solvent recovery, optimized pretreatment, and fluidized-bed pyrolysis, with the review reporting up to 70% glucose recovery for acid hydrolysis and about 20% less energy use for enzymatic recycling than conventional methods [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. The papers also agree that textile waste is technically difficult to process because of mixed fibers, finishes, dyes, and additives, so pretreatment, enzyme time, and repeated treatment may be needed to make conversion efficient [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000]. On the adsorption side, the strongest evidence comes from textile wastewater treatment, where adsorption is described as one of the most feasible ways to remove dyes and metals because it is cost-effective and can use a variety of adsorbents [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. That same paper places adsorption within a broader treatment train combining primary, secondary, and tertiary phases, emphasizing flexible multi-step treatment for complex effluents and reuse-oriented goals such as zero liquid discharge and resource recovery [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. However, most of the papers do not provide direct evidence that textile materials themselves have adsorption properties for waste conversion, and several summaries explicitly state that adsorption-based use is not described [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports combining conversion technologies for solid textile waste with adsorption-based treatment for textile wastewater, but it does not show a unified adsorption-centered conversion strategy for textile materials [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Textile waste management is increasingly presented as a circular-economy problem that should move from dumping toward reuse, recycling, recovery, and closed-loop systems [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000].

Waste conversion methods can turn textile waste into useful outputs such as recycled fibers, separable product streams, glucose, or bio-oil, depending on the process used [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000].

Chemical and enzymatic recycling are highlighted as practical conversion routes, with acid hydrolysis reported to recover up to 70% glucose and enzymatic recycling using about 20% less energy than conventional methods [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000].

Adsorption is described mainly for textile wastewater treatment, where it is considered feasible for removing dyes and metals because it is cost-effective and adaptable to different adsorbents [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000].

Several papers state that mixed fibers, dyes, finishes, and additives complicate textile recycling or conversion, so pretreatment, enzymatic time, and repeated processing may be needed [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is uneven: adsorption is discussed clearly for wastewater treatment, but not as a property of textile waste materials themselves for conversion purposes [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000].

Several summaries explicitly note that they do not provide specific adsorption-based methods, so the adsorption side of the query cannot be answered in a material-conversion sense from most papers [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4283362208||ABSTRACT||000].

The conversion findings are broad and process-focused, but the summaries provide limited comparative detail across methods, so it is hard to determine which approach is best for different textile waste streams [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000].

Some papers emphasize sustainability and circularity at a conceptual level rather than reporting direct implementation outcomes, so practical scalability remains only partially supported by the provided evidence [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How is the translational regulation of NEDD4 linked to the IGF1 signaling pathway, and what does the context say about NEDD4 in cells that depend on this pathway?
draft_answer: The strongest evidence connecting NEDD4 to the IGF1 pathway comes from the gastric cancer study, which divided GC cell lines into IGF1R-dependent and IGF1R-independent groups based on Akt phosphorylation after OSI906 treatment [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000]. In that context, Dox-induced NEDD4 knockdown reduced tumor growth only in IGF1R-dependent cells, while NEDD4 overexpression promoted their growth, indicating that NEDD4’s effect is selective for cells reliant on IGF1/IGF1R signaling [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000]. The same study reports that NEDD4’s translational regulation is linked to the IGF1 pathway through a PTEN-IRS1 axis, and rescue experiments showed this axis is required for NEDD4-mediated regulation of Akt activation and tumor growth [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. It further concludes that NEDD4 promotes proliferation of GC cells dependent on IGF1/IGF1R signaling by antagonizing PTEN’s protein phosphatase activity to IRS1 [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. In that IGF1-related setting, NEDD4 was higher in IGF1-high GC tissues than in IGF1-low or normal tissues, and co-high expression of NEDD4 and IGF1 predicted worse prognosis [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, another cancer study found NEDD4 to be translationally upregulated in pancreatic cancer cells through an undefined translational activation mechanism and linked it to PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling rather than IGF1 signaling [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. That pancreatic study also reported heterogeneous but elevated NEDD4 expression versus normal ductal epithelial cells, and NEDD4 depletion reduced proliferation and migration of PDAC cells [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. Other provided papers do not add evidence for an IGF1–NEDD4 link, instead discussing unrelated systems such as DYRK3/SNAPIN or Nedd4-2 in glutamate transporter regulation [pmc_PMC9803678||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that translational upregulation of NEDD4 can support growth signaling, but the direct IGF1 connection is specifically demonstrated in IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells and not established in the other summaries [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: In gastric cancer cells, NEDD4 knockdown reduced tumor growth only in IGF1R-dependent cells, while NEDD4 overexpression promoted their growth [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000].

NEDD4’s translational regulation is linked to the IGF1 signaling pathway through a PTEN-IRS1 axis, which is required for NEDD4-mediated regulation of Akt activation and tumor growth [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].
The study concludes that NEDD4 promotes proliferation of GC cells dependent on IGF1/IGF1R signaling by antagonizing PTEN’s protein phosphatase activity to IRS1 [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].
NEDD4 was higher in IGF1-high gastric cancer tissues than in IGF1-low or normal tissues, and co-high expression of NEDD4 and IGF1 predicted worse prognosis [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].

In pancreatic cancer cells, NEDD4 was translationally upregulated by an undefined translational activation mechanism and was linked to PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling rather than IGF1 signaling [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The IGF1-linked mechanism for NEDD4 is supported mainly by one gastric cancer study, so the broader generality of this relationship across other cell types is uncertain [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].

The pancreatic cancer study reports translational upregulation of NEDD4 but does not identify the translational mechanism, leaving the upstream control unresolved [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001].
