query: How doeas sustainable marketing relate to enviromental sustainability in shaping a company"s image, and what kinds of consumption changes are described as ways to advance sufficiency transitions?
draft_answer: Across the papers, sustainable marketing is generally presented as a way for firms to align their market activities with environmental sustainability while also strengthening how they are perceived by consumers and the market [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||001]. One paper says green/sustainable marketing demonstrates commitment to sustainability, gives competitive advantage, favors the company’s image, and positions the organization as socio-environmentally responsible [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001]. Another adds that sustainable marketing can build stronger relationships with environmentally conscious consumers by adapting to their preferences and values, supporting long-term success and positive change in the market [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||001]. Several papers also link sustainable marketing to environmental sustainability through pro-sustainable behavior, sustainable consumption patterns, and broader sustainability frameworks that orient marketing toward sustainability and sufficiency [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one paper warns that profit-centric firms may greenwash by inauthentically mimicking sustain-centric practices, suggesting that sustainable marketing can help shape image but also damage credibility when it is not genuine [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also shows tension between growth-oriented approaches and more radical alternatives: one paper describes a dominant profit-centric triple bottom line approach, while another argues for a sustain-centric or degrowth framework because current sustainability debates contain contradictions when growth is reconciled with sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000]. On sufficiency transitions, the evidence consistently mentions sustainable consumption, pro-sustainable behaviour, sustainability, and sufficiency as desired directions, but most summaries do not specify concrete consumption shifts beyond these broad terms [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Sustainable/green marketing is described as signaling commitment to sustainability, supporting a competitive advantage, and improving a company’s image as socio-environmentally responsible [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001].
Sustainable marketing can strengthen relationships with environmentally conscious consumers by adapting to their values and preferences [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||001].

Some summaries frame sustainable marketing as part of broader sustainability communication that promotes sustainable consumption and pro-sustainable behaviour [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000].

A sustain-centric or degrowth-oriented view is contrasted with a profit-centric approach, because current debates are said to contain tensions and contradictions around reconciling growth with sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence mentions sustainable consumption patterns, sustainability, sufficiency, degrowth-minded policies, and transformative frameworks as directions for sufficiency transitions, but does not detail specific consumption changes [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Most summaries describe broad directions such as sustainable consumption, pro-sustainable behaviour, or sufficiency, but they do not specify concrete consumption changes or transition mechanisms.
Some evidence is conditional or cautionary: one paper warns that sustainability claims may become greenwashing when profit-centric firms imitate sustain-centric practices inauthentically.

The summaries vary in how directly they address company image, and several explicitly note that the evidence does not provide a detailed explanation beyond general links to consumer perception or legitimacy.
Several papers report that evidence is insufficient for the second part of the query, so conclusions about sufficiency-transition consumption changes remain limited.

query: How sustainability reporting link with SDGs and sustainability performance, it matter from the supply chain framework too?
draft_answer: Across the papers, sustainability reporting is consistently presented as a way to connect business activity with the SDGs and to assess sustainability performance, but the strength of that connection varies by context and method. Several studies report a positive linkage: sustainability reporting can be monitored with reference to the SDGs to help investors and stakeholders assess firms’ sustainable performance [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001], and integrated reporting is framed as a corporate strategy for achieving SDGs while evaluating implementation with shared metrics [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000]. Other work also finds that sustainability reporting is linked to performance improvement, including through environmental performance measurement, SDG implementation, and materiality matrices that incorporate stakeholder views [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001]. From a supply chain perspective, the evidence suggests this matters a lot: a sustainable supply chain is positively associated with financial performance and with SDGs, and the study explicitly argues that SMEs should implement sustainability from supplier to customer [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001]. A supply-chain sustainability assessment framework built from GRI indicators similarly aims to measure both firms’ and suppliers’ performance and improve transparency and accountability in global supply chains [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. However, not all evidence is aligned: one study finds no correlation in reporting specific SDGs and a disconnection between corporate sustainability performance and SDG reporting, suggesting companies may report SDGs arbitrarily rather than based on actual performance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000]. This is echoed by another study showing that companies may cite SDGs in reports without explaining how sustainability initiatives translate into an actual contribution [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature therefore supports the idea that sustainability reporting can be useful for SDG alignment and performance assessment, but it also warns that reporting quality, indicator selection, and transparency are often weak and need clearer guidance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Sustainability reporting is used to link firms’ activities to the SDGs and to assess sustainable performance [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000].

Several studies report positive relationships among sustainability reporting, sustainability performance, and SDG-related implementation or measurement [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001].

The supply chain framework matters because studies show sustainability assessment tools can measure both firms’ and suppliers’ performance and improve transparency in global supply chains [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001].

Some evidence finds weak or missing alignment between SDG reporting and actual sustainability performance, including no correlation among reported SDGs and a gap between cited SDGs and explained contributions [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000].

A review of sustainable supply chain management found a lack of concrete frameworks and called for clearer sustainability measurement indices, while proposing a framework for achieving SDGs through SSCM [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Some studies do not provide explicit evidence on supply chain frameworks, so the supply-chain connection cannot be generalized to all reporting contexts [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence includes contradictory findings: some papers report positive links between reporting, SDGs, and performance, while others find disconnection or arbitrary SDG selection in reports [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000].

Several summaries explicitly note methodological or conceptual gaps, such as the absence of harmonized ways to connect SDGs with LCSA and the lack of concrete SSCM frameworks or clearer sustainability indicators [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000].

One study highlights that some items had no direct or indirect connection to any SDG because of limited life-cycle-thinking and insufficient discussion for stakeholders such as workers, consumers, and value chain actors [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do the circular economy and sustainable recycling approaches in textile waste and polymeric membranes reduce environmental impact?
draft_answer: Across the textile papers, the circular economy is presented as a way to reduce environmental harm by moving away from a linear model that drives wasteful production and disposal toward reduce, reuse, recycle, repair, repurpose, rental, and resale strategies that extend product life and cut waste [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries state that these approaches reduce the need for new raw materials, lower water, resource, and energy consumption, and turn waste into useful outputs such as recycled yarn, regenerated fibers, biodegradable composites, biofuels, and recycled fiber [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. The textile literature also emphasizes that recycling concepts and technologies are intended to protect resources, the environment, and people, with bio-based recycling highlighted as especially promising because its selectivity and benign processing conditions can help circularize the textile life cycle [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence notes important barriers: recycling is limited by technological and awareness constraints, requires substantial investment and supportive policy, and prior studies have sometimes overlooked its limitations [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4283362208||ABSTRACT||001]. The papers also link these textile strategies to broader sustainability goals, including responsible consumption and production and transparent supply chains through IoT traceability [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000]. For polymeric membranes and plastics, the summary evidence is narrower but similarly frames chemical and biological recycling methods such as pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation as more efficient and sustainable than traditional mechanical recycling, because they support closed-loop circular plastic economy strategies and reduce the environmental burden of persistent polymer waste [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainable recycling reduces environmental impact mainly by diverting waste from disposal, recovering value from discarded materials, and decreasing demand for virgin inputs, but they also show that implementation depends on better technologies, policy support, and design for end-of-life recycling [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: Circular economy approaches in textiles reduce environmental impact by extending product life through reuse, repair, recycling, repurposing, rental, and resale, thereby cutting waste and impact from fast-fashion-driven turnover [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000].

Bio-based recycling is described as a promising textile sustainability strategy because its selectivity and benign processing conditions can help circularize the textile life cycle and reduce environmental impacts [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000].

Textile waste recycling can reduce pollution and resource waste by converting post-consumer textiles into recycled fiber, which lessens the need for new raw materials and diverts waste from disposal [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000].

For polymeric wastes, chemical and biological recycling methods such as pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation are presented as more efficient and sustainable alternatives to traditional mechanical recycling within a circular economy [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000].

The textile papers report that recycling can be limited by technological and awareness barriers and may require substantial investment and supportive policy to be effective [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence on polymeric membranes is limited; the available summary discusses polymers/plastics broadly rather than textile-membrane-specific recycling outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000].

Several textile papers describe barriers such as technological limits, awareness gaps, and the need for policy support, so the environmental benefits may not be fully realized in practice [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001].
One summary notes that prior studies overlooked recycling limitations, suggesting the literature may still understate implementation challenges [https://openalex.org/W4283362208||ABSTRACT||001].

The provided evidence is mostly review-level or summary-level, so it supports general conclusions about environmental impact reduction but not precise comparative effect sizes [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?
draft_answer: Textile waste management can use waste conversion as a way to move away from dumping and toward recovery, reprocessing, reuse, recycling, and circular-economy loops [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers describe conversion routes that turn textile waste into valuable products, including biological treatment with micro-organisms and enzymes, chemical and biotechnological conversion to new products and clean energy, and recycling into recovered fibers such as FINEX fiber [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. One study reports enzymatic deconstruction of cut fabrics into purified fiber fractions, showing that 100% cotton fabrics could be completely disintegrated into slurry and water-soluble degradation products under aggressive mechanical agitation plus cellulase hydrolysis [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000]. The same study also shows that waste conversion is not straightforward because blended fibers and dyes/finishing chemicals interfere with recycling, and reactive dyes inhibited degradation, although longer time, more enzyme, and repeated treatment could reduce those barriers [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the reviews, the common message is that textile waste treatment should combine multiple modalities rather than rely on a single route, because there is no universally applicable solution for textile effluents or wastes [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. In wastewater and effluent management, adsorption is highlighted as one of the most feasible methods for dye and metal removal because it is comparatively cost-effective and can use a variety of adsorbents [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. This means textile waste management can use adsorption mainly as a treatment step for contaminated wastewater streams, while conversion routes handle the solid textile waste itself by turning it into reusable materials, bio-products, or energy [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. The overall direction supported by these papers is an integrated system that combines eco-design, efficient waste management, regenerative production, and bio-based or chemical recycling to reduce pollution and dependence on virgin materials [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Textile waste management is increasingly framed as a shift from dumping to recovery, reprocessing, reuse, recycling, and circular-economy loops [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000].

Waste conversion can transform textile waste into valuable products, clean energy, or recovered fiber fractions through biological, chemical, and enzymatic processes [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000].

Enzymatic deconstruction can completely disintegrate 100% cotton fabrics into slurry and water-soluble degradation products, but blended fibers and dyes/finishing chemicals make recycling harder [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000].

Adsorption is presented as a feasible and cost-advantaged method for removing dyes and metals from textile wastewater, especially when combined with other treatment stages [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000].

There is no universally applicable solution for textile effluents, so the literature recommends combining multiple treatment modalities to meet reuse and resource-recovery goals [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries explicitly note that they do not provide adsorption-specific evidence for textile solids, so adsorption is supported mainly for wastewater treatment rather than for direct solid-waste conversion [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How is the translational regulation of NEDD4 linked to the IGF1 signaling pathway, and what does the context say about NEDD4 in cells that depend on this pathway?
draft_answer: The evidence links translational regulation of NEDD4 to IGF1 signaling most directly in gastric cancer cells, where NEDD4 was shown to be translationally relevant to pathway-dependent growth and Akt activation rather than simply transcriptionally changed [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. In that study, GC cell lines were classified as IGF1R-dependent or IGF1R-independent based on Akt phosphorylation after OSI906 treatment, and NEDD4 knockdown or overexpression altered tumor growth only in the IGF1R-dependent cells [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000]. The mechanism described involved a PTEN-IRS1 axis, with NEDD4 antagonizing PTEN phosphatase activity toward IRS1 to promote Akt activation and proliferation in IGF1/IGF1R-dependent cells [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. Clinically, NEDD4 was reported to be higher in IGF1-high gastric cancer tissues than in IGF1-low and normal tissues, and co-high expression of NEDD4 and IGF1 predicted worse prognosis [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. A related but distinct pancreatic cancer study also found NEDD4 to be translationally upregulated, with polysomal profiling supporting translational activation as the basis for higher protein expression, although that paper linked NEDD4 to PTEN/PI3K/AKT rather than IGF1 signaling specifically [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. In PDAC cells, NEDD4 was significantly higher than in normal pancreatic ductal epithelial cells, and depleting NEDD4 reduced proliferation and migration, suggesting that cells relying on this axis are sensitive to NEDD4 loss [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, another paper in Parkinson’s disease focused on Nedd4-2-mediated ubiquitination of glutamate transporters and did not address IGF1 signaling, highlighting that NEDD4 family members can act in different pathways depending on context [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the strongest supported connection is that translationally upregulated NEDD4 promotes growth in IGF1/IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells, while evidence from other systems shows pathway-specific roles for NEDD4 but does not extend the IGF1 link beyond the gastric cancer context [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In gastric cancer cell lines, NEDD4 affected tumor growth only in IGF1R-dependent cells, which were defined by Akt phosphorylation after OSI906 treatment [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000].
NEDD4 promoted proliferation of IGF1/IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells by antagonizing PTEN activity toward IRS1 and thereby supporting Akt activation [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].
NEDD4 was higher in IGF1-high gastric cancer tissues than in IGF1-low and normal tissues, and co-high NEDD4/IGF1 expression predicted worse prognosis [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].

In PDAC, NEDD4 was translationally upregulated, with polysomal profiling indicating translational activation as the basis for increased protein expression [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001].

In PDAC cells, NEDD4 was elevated relative to normal pancreatic ductal epithelial cells, and NEDD4 depletion reduced proliferation and migration [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001].

The Parkinson’s disease paper discussed Nedd4-2-mediated ubiquitination of glutamate transporters and did not mention IGF1 signaling, showing that the supplied evidence supports pathway-specific rather than universal NEDD4 functions [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The direct mechanistic link between translational regulation of NEDD4 and IGF1 signaling is only described in the gastric cancer paper; the PDAC paper supports translational upregulation of NEDD4 but not an IGF1 connection [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000].

The supplied summaries do not provide detailed experimental methods for the translational mechanism in the IGF1-related study, so the exact upstream regulators of NEDD4 translation remain unclear [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001].
Evidence from other papers is context-specific and does not generalize to IGF1-dependent cells, limiting how broadly the findings can be applied [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000].

The summaries do not indicate whether the IGF1-associated NEDD4 findings were validated in non-gastric models, so the pathway relationship may be disease-context dependent [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
draft_answer: Across these papers, the SDGs are presented as a central reference point for policy coherence for sustainable development in the EU, because they can be used to align EU and national priorities with the broader 2030 Agenda [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies frame coherence operationally: one maps the SDGs against the European Green Deal, the European Semester, Country-Specific Recommendations, and recovery planning to improve alignment across policy frameworks [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000], while another argues that a system perspective is needed to boost coherence across governance levels and scales of implementation [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001]. Other papers connect coherence to monitoring and evidence, suggesting that circular economy implementation, lifecycle assessment, and SDG tracking can help assess whether policy goals support each other and stay within planetary limits [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature does not present SDG-based coherence as purely technical: one paper argues that incoherencies are fundamentally political and that “neutral” or “win-win” institutional arrangements can obscure conflict and limit transformative change [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Empirically, the evidence suggests uneven coherence across the EU, since environmental SDGs are described as the most complex and least coherent [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000], and some major sustainability challenges are not captured by the Country-Specific Recommendations even when the EU has generally incorporated the SDGs into strategic priorities [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. The papers also point to data and research gaps, including poor intra-cluster connections around the SDGs and the need for more transdisciplinary research [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001], as well as the need for better data availability and monitoring to support coherence [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that in the EU context the SDGs link to policy coherence both as a coordinating framework for aligning agendas and as a monitoring lens for detecting trade-offs, but their effectiveness depends on political context, institutional design, and the completeness of the underlying evidence base [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In the EU context, the SDGs are used as a reference for aligning national and EU policy priorities with the broader 2030 Agenda [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000].

Policy coherence is operationalized through mapping and alignment tools that connect the SDGs with the European Green Deal, the European Semester, Country-Specific Recommendations, and recovery plans [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000].

Lifecycle assessment can support EU policy design and monitoring by linking EU policy, the SDGs, and planetary boundaries, although those interlinkages are uneven across frameworks [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000].

The literature also warns that SDG-based policy coherence can mask political conflict, because incoherencies are not only technical but also political [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

Environmental SDGs are described as the most complex and least coherent in the EU, indicating that coherence challenges are especially pronounced in biodiversity and climate-related areas [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence base suggests a need for more transdisciplinary research and better data and monitoring to strengthen policy coherence across SDG-related areas in the EU [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001], [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The studies use different conceptual lenses and tools (mapping, lifecycle assessment, governance theory, monitoring), so their findings are not directly comparable across all EU policy domains.
Several summaries note that coherence is uneven or incomplete, but the evidence does not provide a single EU-wide measure of policy coherence across all SDGs.
One paper explicitly cautions that institutional arrangements may create an apolitical façade, suggesting that apparent coherence may hide unresolved political trade-offs.
Some evidence is based on specific cases or subsets of goals, such as the Netherlands, environmental SDGs, SDG 9, or SDG 11, limiting how broadly the findings can be generalized to the whole EU.

query: How are Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) and optimization used in sustainability evaluation frameworks for transport systems, and what methods are highlighted for road transport sustainability analysis?
draft_answer: Across the reviewed transport-sustainability papers, MCDM/MCDA is consistently used to handle the fact that transport systems must be evaluated across multiple, often conflicting criteria rather than by a single score alone [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000]. One review explicitly states that MCDM is the preferred framework type for public transport sustainability evaluation, with AHP the most frequently used method, while another argues that sustainability assessment is increasingly moving from classic sustainability indices toward MCDA methods that should be matched to the decision problem and context [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000]. Several frameworks operationalize this by integrating indicators into a single sustainability index, such as the STPI for public transport, or by combining social, economic, and environmental factors through MCDM and normalization procedures [https://openalex.org/W4363679553||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also emphasizes that method choice matters: one framework analyzes 28 MCDA methods to identify which are most suitable under different sustainability decision characteristics, and another notes that normalization technique can materially affect robustness and reliability [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000]. In applied transport cases, MCDM is used not only for ranking alternatives but also for weighting criteria and structuring complex decisions, as shown by the integrated entropy–CoCoSo framework for road transport sustainability in OECD countries and the spherical fuzzy SWARA–MARCOS model for sustainable vehicle prioritization in Tehran [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320918985||ABSTRACT||000]. For road transport sustainability analysis specifically, the highlighted methods are entropy-based objective weighting and CoCoSo ranking, with entropy reducing subjectivity and CoCoSo producing the final performance order [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000]. Other transport studies show hybrid workflows as well, such as DEMATEL, REMBRANDT, and VIKOR in an expressway placement case, with results compared against EIA and alternative methods including AHP, Fuzzy AHP, TOPSIS, and PROMETHEE [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that MCDM helps stakeholders compare sustainability dimensions, but they differ in whether the main contribution is a general method-selection framework, a composite index, or a specific ranking/weighting hybrid for a transport subdomain [https://openalex.org/W4378909343||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4366259790||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: MCDM/MCDA is widely used in transport sustainability evaluation because it can combine multiple conflicting criteria into a single assessment or ranking [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000].
A review of public transport sustainability frameworks found MCDM to be the preferred framework type, with AHP the most frequently used MCDM method [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000].
For road transport sustainability analysis, the highlighted methods are entropy-based objective weighting and CoCoSo ranking [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000].

One transport sustainability framework combines existing discrete indexes into the Sustainable Transport Planning Index (STPI) using AHP, expert judgment, normalization, and weighted averaging [https://openalex.org/W4363679553||ABSTRACT||000].

A hybrid expressway-placement study used DEMATEL, REMBRANDT, and VIKOR, and compared the resulting ranking with EIA and with AHP, Fuzzy AHP, TOPSIS, and PROMETHEE [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000].

Method selection and normalization are presented as important determinants of credible sustainability evaluation results [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is drawn from abstracts and review summaries, so it provides limited detail on implementation, validation, and comparative performance of the methods.
Road transport findings are specific to the cited OECD and vehicle-prioritization studies, so they may not generalize to all road transport contexts.
Some papers emphasize composite indices, while others emphasize ranking/weighting hybrids, so the literature does not converge on a single best framework.
The provided summaries note gaps in some regions and applications, including explicit gaps for Latin American public transport frameworks.

query: How does the theme of "Green Cluod Computing" connect the discussion of Green IoT with the systematic survey of energy-efficient techniques in sustainabl cloud computing, especially regarding why data centers and cloud technologies are being optimized for lower energy use and reduced environmental harm?
draft_answer: Green IoT and Green Cloud Computing are linked in the summaries as parts of a broader ICT sustainability agenda aimed at reducing energy consumption, carbon emissions, pollution, and other environmental harms [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||001]. The cloud-computing papers explain why this matters: growing numbers of networked devices and cloud services are driving up data-center power use, heat generation, cooling needs, and carbon emissions, so future cloud systems must become energy-efficient and environmentally sustainable [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the survey-oriented summaries, the optimization goal is consistent: reduce electricity use and environmental harm through techniques such as VM virtualization and consolidation, power-aware methods, bio-inspired approaches, thermal management, and integrated workload/resource management [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000]. The data-center-focused papers further show that this push is not only about emissions, but also about operational sustainability, since greener infrastructure can lower operating costs, improve resource efficiency, and support regulatory compliance and brand benefits [https://openalex.org/W4391045525||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4366762583||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries also emphasize that software-level and orchestration-level techniques are attractive because they can require less infrastructure and be less failure-prone, which helps explain why cloud technologies are often optimized through management and control rather than only by hardware replacement [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||001]. More recent framing expands this idea beyond the cloud alone, describing sustainability as something integrated across design, development, monitoring, refactoring, compliance, and Kubernetes-style resource management [https://openalex.org/W4391566264||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the theme of “Green Cloud Computing” connects Green IoT to sustainable cloud surveys by treating the cloud and its data centers as the energy-hungry backbone of connected systems that must be redesigned for lower energy use and reduced environmental harm [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Green IoT is presented as relying on Green Cloud Computing and Green Data Centers as enabling ICT technologies within a broader sustainability agenda [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||001].

Cloud computing and data centers are being optimized because rising use of ICT, cloud services, and networked devices increases energy demand, heat, cooling problems, and carbon emissions [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000].

Greener cloud/data-center operations are also linked to operational benefits such as lower operating costs, better brand image, and regulatory compliance [https://openalex.org/W4391045525||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4366762583||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do sustainable technologies, such as clean energy in manufacturing and green and reverse logistics, support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises, and what did the analysis find about enterprise adoption and environmental management?
draft_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies are consistently presented as enabling Industry 4.0 innovation while also supporting broader sustainability and SDG-related growth in industrial enterprises [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. In particular, clean energy in manufacturing, green logistics, and reverse logistics are described as conditions that can foster industry development and future growth through Industry 4.0 technologies and innovations in an SDG context [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. Multiple reviews similarly conclude that Industry 4.0 can improve environmental sustainability by increasing manufacturing efficiency, reducing resource consumption, and strengthening environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. The literature also frames Industry 4.0 and sustainability as mutually reinforcing: sustainability can guide technology development, and those technologies can strengthen sustainability pillars and reduce environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282842216||ABSTRACT||001]. Evidence on enterprise behavior is strongest in the Slovakia-based analysis of 105 enterprises, where more than 82% reported implementing the SDGs and more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That study also found significant relationships between environmental management and sustainability in production and logistics, including a confirmed link between renewable energy technology use in the industrial sector and sustainability in logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the broader review literature is more cautious and notes that some Industry 4.0 technologies can also create environmental harms such as air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive use of raw materials, information, and energy, indicating a gap between intended and actual sustainable practice [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests a positive but conditional relationship: sustainable technologies and Industry 4.0 together can support SDG-based growth and environmental improvement, yet adoption and environmental management outcomes appear uneven and context-dependent, especially outside the few studies that report enterprise-level data [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Clean energy in manufacturing, green logistics, and reverse logistics are described as supporting industry development and future growth through Industry 4.0 technologies and SDG-oriented innovation [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

A review of 105 Slovak enterprises found that more than 82% implemented the SDGs and more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

The same enterprise analysis reported significant relationships between environmental management and sustainability in production and logistics, including a confirmed relationship between renewable energy technology use and sustainability in logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

Several reviews conclude that Industry 4.0 improves environmental sustainability by increasing efficiency, reducing resource consumption, and supporting sustainable manufacturing and environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001].

The literature also warns that some Industry 4.0 technologies can negatively affect environmental sustainability through pollution, waste disposal problems, and excessive consumption of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000].

Sustainability and digitisation are presented as a combined approach for industrial transformation and innovation in manufacturing, with sustainability used both to guide technology development and to strengthen sustainability pillars [https://openalex.org/W4282842216||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Only one summary provides enterprise-level adoption data; most papers are literature reviews or conceptual analyses and do not report direct adoption rates or operational outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000].

Several summaries explicitly state that they do not provide detailed findings on clean energy in manufacturing, green and reverse logistics, or environmental management, limiting how far the evidence can be generalized [https://openalex.org/W3120619572||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4282842216||ABSTRACT||001].

The evidence base is uneven across contexts, with some findings coming from Slovakia, the UAE, or India, so cross-country generalization is uncertain [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120619572||ABSTRACT||000].

There is a tension in the literature between the view that Industry 4.0 supports sustainability and the finding that it can also generate environmental harms, so the net effect appears context-dependent rather than uniformly positive [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How was ARDL used to test the nexus, and what long-run association did it reveal for human capital and renewable energy?
draft_answer: The clearest evidence shows that ARDL was used in a China-based study to test the nexus among variables after first checking stationarity with the augmented Dickey-Fuller test, and the same study covered data from 1986–2019 [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. In that analysis, ARDL results indicated that human capital, renewable energy consumption, and renewable energy production were negatively associated with carbon emissions and positively associated with sustainable development goals [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. A related China study also used ARDL, together with ADF and Granger causality, to evaluate associations and directional nexus over 1986–2019, but it did not mention human capital, so it cannot be used to specify a human-capital/renewable-energy long-run result [https://openalex.org/W4315784444||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers in the set used variants or related models such as CS-ARDL, nonlinear ARDL, and dynamic ARDL simulations, but their abstracts either focused on different variables or did not report a human-capital-specific long-run association with renewable energy [https://openalex.org/W4388450586||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206606027||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4315629505||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports that ARDL was used as a nexus-testing framework in at least one empirical study, but the provided summaries do not separately report a distinct long-run estimate specifically for the relationship between human capital and renewable energy [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. Thus, the long-run implication available from the summaries is only the broader positive association of human capital and renewable energy variables with sustainable development outcomes and their negative association with carbon emissions, rather than a standalone human-capital-renewable-energy coefficient [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: A China study used the augmented Dickey-Fuller test for stationarity and then ARDL to test the nexus among variables over 1986–2019 [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000].

In that ARDL analysis, human capital, renewable energy consumption, and renewable energy production were negatively associated with carbon emissions and positively associated with sustainable development goals [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000].

Another China study also used ARDL with ADF and Granger causality to evaluate associations and directional nexus, but it did not mention human capital [https://openalex.org/W4315784444||ABSTRACT||000].

CS-ARDL, nonlinear ARDL, and dynamic ARDL simulations appear in other abstracts, but those studies either focus on different variables or do not report a human-capital-specific long-run association with renewable energy [https://openalex.org/W4388450586||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206606027||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4315629505||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The summaries do not provide a separate long-run coefficient specifically for human capital and renewable energy, so that exact nexus cannot be precisely stated.
Most evidence comes from China-focused studies, limiting how broadly the findings can be generalized.
Several abstracts mention ARDL variants or related methods but do not report the specific nexus result asked about, leaving the evidence incomplete.

query: In the context of Sustainable Consumption, what did the systematic review conclude about the concept’s complexity, its relationship to the circular economy, and the role of government in supporting sustainable consumption?
draft_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable consumption is presented as a complex and still-developing concept rather than a single, settled idea, with one review explicitly calling it a “complex and nebulous concept” whose theoretical fragmentation creates overlapping concepts [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000]. Related reviews reinforce this complexity by showing that sustainability indicators for the circular economy are incomplete, that simple circularity metrics are insufficient, and that assessment must consider multiple dimensions rather than circularity alone [https://openalex.org/W3163949760||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3120864615||ABSTRACT||000]. The relationship between sustainable consumption and the circular economy is consistently portrayed as close and important, but also difficult: one review links consumers directly to the circular economy while noting the challenges of that interaction [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000], and others describe the circular economy as an emerging field with limited theory and research, contested visions, and technocentric tendencies that can overlook social and ecological implications [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4378216524||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers also caution that circularity does not automatically equal sustainability, because some “sustainable” practices may still harm environment or society, and increased circularity can create unintended externalities [https://openalex.org/W3132132623||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120864615||ABSTRACT||000]. On the question of government, the systematic review literature indicates that government matters as part of the support structure for sustainable consumption, including its role and tools in the discussion of the concept [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers are more specific that sustainable circular transitions require collaboration among businesses, governments, and stakeholders, and that without policy steer and public support, the transition may fail to achieve sustainable outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4409544928||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4289130621||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the literature converges on the view that sustainable consumption is inherently interdisciplinary, tightly linked to circular economy debates, and dependent on government involvement, but it also shows that the field remains theoretically fragmented and empirically underdeveloped [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Sustainable consumption is described as a complex and nebulous concept with theoretical fragmentation that creates overlapping concepts [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000].

The relationship between sustainable consumption and the circular economy is close but difficult, with the consumer–circular economy link explicitly noted as challenging [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000].

Circular economy is repeatedly presented as emerging, contested, and insufficient on its own as a sustainability guarantee, because circularity can still produce unintended externalities or harmful outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120864615||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132132623||ABSTRACT||000].

Government is portrayed as an important supporter of sustainable consumption and circular transitions, including through government tools, policy steer, and collaboration with other stakeholders [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4409544928||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4289130621||ABSTRACT||001].

The literature notes a research gap and limited theoretical and empirical development in circular economy-related work, which reinforces the field’s uncertainty [https://openalex.org/W3163949760||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries do not provide direct evidence on sustainable consumption itself, so some conclusions are inferred from circular economy literature rather than stated explicitly [https://openalex.org/W3132132623||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence on government support is general rather than detailed; it mentions government roles, policy steer, and collaboration, but does not specify which policies or tools are most effective [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4409544928||ABSTRACT||001].

The literature is still described as theoretically fragmented, contested, and empirically limited, so the relationship between sustainable consumption and circular economy remains incompletely resolved [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000].

query: What clinical and laboratory findings are associated with elevated FSH in men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, and how do KS and testicular XX DSD compare with the undefined cause group?
draft_answer: In men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA), elevated FSH is associated with poorer sperm retrieval outcomes, and failed retrieval is also linked to elevated LH, whereas successful retrieval is linked to larger testicular volume, a higher testosterone-to-LH ratio, and bilateral testicular volumes as significant predictors in multivariate analysis [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||000]. In the subgroup of men with NOA and chromosomal anomalies, Klinefelter syndrome (KS) is characterized by lower average testicular volume, shorter penile length, lower total testosterone, greater height and arm span, higher LH and FSH, and more frequent gynecomastia [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, men with testicular XX DSD show LH, FSH, and penile length values intermediate between the KS and undefined-cause groups, with testicular volume similar to the KS group but other data similar to the undefined-cause group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. The same study concludes that clinical and laboratory data can distinguish men with NOA and chromosomal anomalies, especially KS and testicular XX, from those with undefined causes [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the provided evidence does not give subgroup-specific FSH-outcome data for KS versus testicular XX DSD beyond these comparative baseline findings [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. Another paper in this set addresses chromosomal abnormalities and AZF screening indications in NOA/severe oligozoospermia but does not report FSH-related clinical findings or KS/testicular XX DSD comparisons [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: In NOA, elevated serum FSH and LH are associated with failed sperm retrieval, while larger testicular volume and a higher testosterone-to-LH ratio are associated with successful retrieval [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||000].

Among men with NOA and chromosomal anomalies, KS is associated with higher FSH, higher LH, lower testicular volume, shorter penile length, lower total testosterone, greater height and arm span, and more frequent gynecomastia than the undefined-cause group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001].

Testicular XX DSD shows LH, FSH, and penile length values intermediate between KS and the undefined-cause group, with testicular volume similar to KS and the remaining data similar to the undefined-cause group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001].
The study of NOA with chromosomal anomalies concludes that clinical and laboratory data can distinguish KS and testicular XX DSD from men with undefined causes [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001].

The AZF-screening paper identifies certain chromosomal abnormalities in NOA/severe oligozoospermia as referral indications, but it does not provide FSH-related findings or KS/testicular XX DSD comparisons [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is limited to abstract-level summaries, so detailed subgroup methods, effect sizes, and thresholds are not available [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001].

Direct FSH-outcome data are available for NOA generally, but not specifically for KS versus testicular XX DSD versus undefined-cause groups [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001].

One paper in the set discusses chromosomal abnormalities and AZF screening but provides no relevant clinical/laboratory comparison for this query, limiting cross-study synthesis [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||001].

No evidence here supports conclusions about other potential clinical or laboratory markers beyond those explicitly reported, and one paper is unrelated to the male infertility question [pmc_PMC10141627||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do Sustainable Catalytric Technologies support global resource securty and sustainability?
draft_answer: Sustainable Catalytric Technologies are presented across these papers as a way to support global resource security and sustainability by reducing dependence on fossil resources, scarce catalysts, and linear resource use patterns [https://openalex.org/W4397002662||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401191227||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries frame catalysis as central to solving interconnected challenges such as climate change, pollution, and sustainable energy, with heterogeneous catalysis described as a key enabler of a sustainable future [https://openalex.org/W3136963614||ABSTRACT||000]. The papers also emphasize that catalyzed chemical transformations powered by renewable electricity can replace fossil fuels without reducing human wellbeing, while electrocatalytic processes can produce solar fuels and commodity chemicals for many sectors [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000]. Resource security is further supported by biomass conversion and waste valorization, which can turn biomass into biofuels and high-value products and help shift industry from a linear to a circular economy [https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4397002662||ABSTRACT||000]. In addition, rational design of earth-abundant catalysts is highlighted as a response to catalyst scarcity, and catalyst design best practices are presented as a way to improve sustainable product development [https://openalex.org/W4401191227||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3214828424||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also links these technologies to long-term system change, arguing that early action is needed to catalyze broader sustainability transitions and meet more ambitious targets by 2050 and 2100 [https://openalex.org/W4284690057||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the papers caution that technical, economic, and societal tradeoffs, as well as infrastructure, feedstock mobilization, techno-economics, and carbon-stock concerns, affect feasibility and acceptance [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385888760||ABSTRACT||000]. Green chemistry and green engineering principles, together with quantitative sustainability analysis, are presented as tools for measuring improvements, identifying remaining problem areas, and guiding research investment and commercialization [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainable catalysis can help secure essential fuels, chemicals, and services while lowering environmental burdens, but they also show that real-world sustainability depends on careful assessment of tradeoffs and broader system conditions [https://openalex.org/W4397002662||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Sustainable catalytic technologies can support resource security by enabling continued production of essential fuels and chemicals while reducing dependence on fossil inputs and waste generation [https://openalex.org/W4397002662||ABSTRACT||000].

Catalysis powered by renewable electricity is described as a route to distributed, affordable, clean energy and to the production of solar fuels and commodity chemicals across multiple sectors [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000].
Rational design of earth-abundant catalysts is presented as a way to overcome catalyst scarcity and strengthen sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4401191227||ABSTRACT||000].

Biomass conversion and biomass valorization can improve biorefinery sustainability by producing biofuels and high-value products and supporting a circular economy [https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4397002662||ABSTRACT||000].

Green chemistry, green engineering, and quantitative sustainability analysis are used to measure improvements, identify remaining problem areas, and inform research and commercialization decisions [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries note tradeoffs and feasibility constraints, including technical, economic, and societal issues, but do not provide detailed quantitative comparisons across technologies [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||000].

Evidence on biomass and bioenergy benefits is paired with warnings about infrastructure, feedstock mobilization, carbon stocks, and trade-related sustainability risks, so benefits may depend strongly on deployment context [https://openalex.org/W4385888760||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||001].

Some papers emphasize long-term sustainability transitions and ambitious future targets, but the summaries do not show measured outcomes at scale or whether these technologies have already achieved those targets [https://openalex.org/W4284690057||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence is broad and conceptual across multiple application areas, but it does not provide direct head-to-head evidence showing which catalytic approach is most effective for global resource security [https://openalex.org/W3136963614||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3214828424||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the sustainability assessment of district heating systems, which multi-criteria decision analysis methods were compared, and what did the sensitivity analysis reveal about their suitability and differences in calculation and interpretation?
draft_answer: In the district-heating sustainability assessment study, five multi-criteria decision analysis methods were compared: WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, using 8 criteria for 12 district heating companies [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The paper reports that sensitivity analysis was used to identify the most credible method by changing criteria weights in three ways: varying them individually across the stability range of alternatives, varying them individually by a fixed amount to examine effects on average scores, and comparing AHP-derived weights with equal weights [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The study and its literature review concluded that all five methods are suitable for sustainability analyses of district heating systems, but they differ in their calculation procedures and in how their results are interpreted [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. This implies that method choice is not about whether the methods can be used at all, but about which one best fits the decision context and how its outputs should be read [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. Broader sustainability-assessment literature is consistent with this contextual view, arguing that MCDA methods should be tailored to the decision situation and that method selection should be guided by methodological features [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000]. Separately, a district-heating sustainability review found MCDM methods were preferred in practice and that AHP was the most frequently used method, but it did not provide the same kind of cross-method sensitivity comparison [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: The district-heating study compared WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA for sustainability assessment using 8 criteria and 12 district heating companies [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

Its sensitivity analysis varied criteria weights in three ways: individually across the stability range of alternatives, individually by a fixed value to assess average-score effects, and by comparing AHP weights with equal weights [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

The study concluded that all five methods are suitable for district-heating sustainability analysis, but they differ in calculation process and interpretation of results [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Only one paper in the provided summaries directly answers the question about comparing methods and sensitivity analysis in district heating, so the synthesis is based mainly on that single source [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

query: Based on the review of "sustainable innovations," what factors are said to encourage or block farmers" adoption of these innovations, and how do environmental values, in contrast with complexity, innovation aversion, and low perceived control, shape this adoption behavior?
draft_answer: Across the reviews, farmers’ adoption of sustainable innovations is described as being encouraged by a mix of innovation characteristics, producer and operation characteristics, and broader social/institutional supports, while being blocked by attributes of the innovation and by farmers’ perceptions and beliefs [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210468156||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4309605934||ABSTRACT||001]. Specifically, adoption is fostered by factors such as specific innovation characteristics, self-efficacy, social-environmental altruism, communication and networking, other conservation practice use, cash-crop diversity, livestock operations, and farming size [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4387228452||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4387228452||ABSTRACT||001]. It is also supported by producer demographics, land tenure, labor and credit availability, participation in demonstration trials, and access to policy frameworks, credit, research, extension services, and consumer demand for sustainably produced food [https://openalex.org/W4210468156||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3174938154||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4383033841||ABSTRACT||002]. In contrast, the review of sustainable innovations identifies innovation complexity, a high degree of innovation aversion, and low perceived control as major barriers to adoption [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000]. Another review similarly argues that adoption is difficult to predict because technology attributes interact with dissemination institutions and farm/farmer-specific variables, and that complexity across sustainable practices can block or complicate adoption [https://openalex.org/W3118303193||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4387228452||ABSTRACT||000]. Environmental values appear to encourage adoption: the review explicitly says environmental values can drive adoption, and it gives organic farmers as an example of actors with a stronger environmental view who place less weight on economic gains [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, this suggests that environmental values can counterbalance barriers such as complexity, innovation aversion, and low perceived control by making farmers more willing to adopt sustainable innovations despite immediate economic tradeoffs [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one meta-analysis notes that methodological factors significantly affect willingness-to-accept estimates, reminding us that some reported adoption evidence is sensitive to study design rather than only substantive determinants [https://openalex.org/W4313535119||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Farmers’ adoption of sustainable innovations is encouraged by innovation characteristics, individual psychological and socio-demographic features, and environmental values [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000].

One study found that external factors did not influence perceived usefulness, but the abstract does not report the coefficient or p-value for that null effect [https://openalex.org/W4318066212||ABSTRACT||001]. In contrast, another SEM study reported that perceived ease of use had a statistically significant impact on perceived usefulness, and that satisfaction, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, information quality, self-efficacy, social influence, and benefits significantly affected students’ behavioral intention to accept the e-learning portal, again without numeric estimates [https://openalex.org/W3169691847||ABSTRACT||001]. A separate SEM-PLS study found that experience, technology anxiety, and facilitating conditions had a favorable impact on task–technology fit and perceived ease of use, while task–technology fit and perceived ease of use positively affected behavioral intention to use and the adoption process, but no coefficients or p-values were given [https://openalex.org/W4200243604||ABSTRACT||000]. Other abstracts similarly report positive effects of system quality, service quality, quality of life, and other quality factors on perceived usefulness, satisfaction, system use, or continued usage intention, but they do not provide the numerical SEM results needed to answer precisely [https://openalex.org/W3193887958||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4283212605||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4285221835||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests mostly positive associations between external factors and e-learning acceptance outcomes, with one null finding for external factors and perceived usefulness, but the exact path coefficients and p-values are unavailable in the provided summaries [https://openalex.org/W4318066212||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3169691847||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4200243604||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: One study reported that external factors did not influence perceived usefulness, but no SEM coefficient or p-value was provided [https://openalex.org/W4318066212||ABSTRACT||001].

Another SEM study found that perceived ease of use significantly affected perceived usefulness, and that satisfaction, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, information quality, self-efficacy, social influence, and benefits significantly affected behavioral intention to accept the e-learning portal, but without path coefficients or p-values [https://openalex.org/W3169691847||ABSTRACT||001].

A SEM-PLS study reported that experience, technology anxiety, and facilitating conditions positively affected task–technology fit and perceived ease of use, and that task–technology fit and perceived ease of use positively affected behavioral intention to use and the adoption process, but no numeric estimates were reported [https://openalex.org/W4200243604||ABSTRACT||000].

Several other abstracts likewise describe positive effects of quality factors on perceived usefulness, satisfaction, system use, or continued usage intention, but they do not provide the SEM path coefficients or p-values [https://openalex.org/W3193887958||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4283212605||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4285221835||ABSTRACT||000].

query: What changes are reshaping the Industrial manufacturing industry, and what should companies focus on to support digital and green transformation?
draft_answer: The papers agree that Industrial manufacturing is being reshaped by digital transformation, the digital economy, and Industry 4.0 technologies such as cloud computing, big data, IoT, AI, and internet-based connectivity, which are changing production methods, management models, and innovation capabilities [https://openalex.org/W4313238684||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4319599463||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3164306258||ABSTRACT||001]. Several papers specifically frame green digital transformation as combining digitalization with green technologies so that business processes, products, and models become environmentally sustainable [https://openalex.org/W3182760100||ABSTRACT||001]. query: How mask mandates help Covid-19 cases, and what did the study find?
draft_answer: Across the relevant studies, mask mandates appear to help reduce COVID-19 spread by lowering infection incidence and by offsetting some of the increase in cases associated with higher mobility and weaker prevention. In a US state-level analysis, a mask mandate could offset about one third of the increase in case growth caused by a one-standard-deviation rise in mobility, and the estimated effect was stronger in states with higher compliance [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. The same study estimated that a national mask mandate starting on May 15, 2020 would have reduced total US infections by 23.7% to 30.4% by November 15, 2020, indicating a substantial population-level benefit [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. Another study found that keeping prevention measures in place for at least 2 months was associated with lower COVID-19 incidence, and this pattern held for face mask mandates specifically [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. That study also reported that the monthly incidence difference associated with sustained mask mandates ranged from about –4 cases per 100,000 in low-vulnerability counties to –401 cases per 100,000 in high-vulnerability counties, suggesting larger benefit in more socially vulnerable communities [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. A separate indoor-environment study found that a face mask combined with upward ventilation reduced infectious concentration by nearly 99.95% compared with no precautions, but also warned that a mask can be counterproductive if it is placed inappropriately with ventilation, implying that masks work best as part of a proper strategy rather than alone [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001]. Supporting the general protective effect of masks, healthcare-worker studies found that face masks and especially N95 or surgical masks provided significant protection against infection, while gloves, gowns, and some other PPE components showed less clear benefit [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests mask mandates help lower COVID-19 cases, particularly when compliance is high, when they are maintained for longer periods, and when paired with other measures such as ventilation [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001].
