limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is drawn from a mix of conceptual papers, reviews, and a small number of empirical contexts, so the synthesis may not generalize across all public authorities or countries [W3147261195||ABSTRACT||000; W4320719832||ABSTRACT||000].

Materiality is described as ambiguous and contested because sustainability issues are complex, interconnected, and long-term, so there is no simple consensus on what should be reported [W4289767614||ABSTRACT||000].

Several summaries note that research in public-sector sustainability reporting is still early-stage and shaped by evolving or mandatory regulation, which limits how definitive the evidence is [W3147261195||ABSTRACT||000; W4313418383||ABSTRACT||001].

One study reports low disclosure quality and shallow diffusion in Indonesian public companies, indicating that public value may depend heavily on implementation quality rather than on reporting alone [W4313418383||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do sustainable technologies and environmantal management relate in the context of Industry 4.0 and SDGs, and what did the study find about enterprises preference for environmental aspects in business management?
draft_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies and environmental management are presented as closely linked in Industry 4.0 because digital and advanced manufacturing technologies are repeatedly described as drivers of sustainability, environmental performance, and SDG-related outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies say Industry 4.0 technologies such as Big Data, IoT, cyber-physical systems, additive manufacturing, and analytics can improve manufacturing efficiency, reduce resource consumption, and support sustainable manufacturing or a sustainable environment [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3120619572||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000]. In the SDG context, the evidence indicates that integrating Industry 4.0 with the SDGs can improve environmental sustainability and create ecological support and better environmental performance, while also helping reshape organizational processes toward sustainability goals [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one paper emphasizes that the relationship between Industry 4.0 and sustainability remains unclear and fragmented in the literature, and another notes that Industry 4.0 technologies can also produce environmental harms such as air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive consumption of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. The papers therefore present a mostly positive but not unqualified view: sustainable technologies are seen as enabling environmental management, yet they may also create environmental risks that need further investigation and better management [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Regarding enterprises’ preference for environmental aspects in business management, the clearest evidence comes from one study reporting that more than 70% of enterprises prefer environmental aspects in business management and more than 82% implement the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That same study also found a significant relationship between enterprise environmental management in the SDG context and sustainability in production and logistics, including a relationship with renewable energy technology use in industry [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers either do not report this preference directly or explicitly state that the evidence is insufficient to determine it [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Industry 4.0 technologies are repeatedly described as supporting sustainability, environmental performance, and SDG-related outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000].

The literature identifies both benefits and environmental risks of Industry 4.0, including possible pollution, waste disposal problems, and excessive use of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000].

Integrating Industry 4.0 with the SDGs is reported to improve environmental sustainability and create ecological support and better environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

One study found a significant relationship between enterprise environmental management in the SDG context and sustainability in production and logistics, including renewable energy technology use in industry [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].
More than 70% of enterprises in one study preferred environmental aspects in business management, and more than 82% implemented the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is uneven across papers: several summaries explicitly say they do not report enterprises’ preference for environmental aspects in business management, so the preference finding is supported by only one study [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000].

The relationship between Industry 4.0 and sustainability is described as unclear and fragmented in parts of the literature, so the overall evidence base is not fully settled [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000].

One study emphasizes that Industry 4.0 can also have negative environmental effects, which means the sustainability benefits are not universal and may depend on implementation and management [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do energy resourses and renewable energy in mining together help with environmental sustainability and sustainable development, and what good effects are said about using renewable energy in mining for sustainability?
draft_answer: Across the papers, energy resources and renewable energy are presented as central to making mining more environmentally sustainable and better aligned with sustainable development goals (SDGs) because mining has high energy demand, often relies on fossil fuels, and produces multiple environmental harms such as greenhouse gas emissions, dust, waste, and other pollution [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000]. A more sustainable mining industry is described as one that reduces resource and energy consumption across all stages of mining, from exploration to post-closure, while also minimizing waste and ecological disturbance [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000]. The strongest reported benefits of renewable energy use in mining are lower carbon emissions, reduced energy usage, improved waste management, and decreased environmental pollution [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000]. One paper also says renewable energy in mining can create jobs, support a circular economy, reduce operating costs, and improve sustainable development indicators [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the evidence is not uniformly positive: another paper warns that sustainability assessments should not focus only on carbon emissions because renewable energy systems can have a “dark side” and may harm other aspects of sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000]. Similarly, one mining sustainability study reports increased air emissions, water use, and energy usage for most companies and an absence of improvement in renewable energy utilization, suggesting that better energy management is still needed [https://openalex.org/W3165375152||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that renewable energy and improved energy management can help mining contribute to environmental sustainability and SDGs, but they also show that benefits depend on broader technological, regulatory, and implementation conditions [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Mining sustainability requires reducing energy and resource consumption across all stages of mining to limit waste and environmental damage [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||000].

Green mining practices that include renewable energy and electric vehicles are reported to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, lower energy consumption, and improve waste management [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000].

Using renewable energy in mining is said to help create jobs, reduce operating costs, support a circular economy, and improve sustainable development indicators [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001].

Renewable energy is important for sustainable development, but one paper cautions that renewables can also have negative sustainability impacts beyond carbon emissions [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000].

A mining sustainability study found increased air emissions, water use, and energy usage for most companies and no improvement in renewable energy utilization, indicating that better energy management is still needed [https://openalex.org/W3165375152||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers are abstract-only summaries, so the evidence is limited and does not provide detailed methods or full context for the claims [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001].

The evidence is mixed: some papers report clear sustainability gains from renewable energy in mining, while another reports no improvement in renewable energy utilization and rising energy use in companies [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3165375152||ABSTRACT||000].

One paper warns that renewable energy can have adverse sustainability effects beyond carbon reduction, so the net environmental benefit may depend on broader lifecycle and system impacts [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000].

At least one summary notes barriers such as limited information, high investment, lack of skilled labor, and high maintenance costs, showing that practical implementation may be difficult [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How the sustainability assessment and evaluation frameworks in the district heating and PT evaluation studies are linked, and which method was most used, plus how do they relate to CO2 emissions reduction in the urban transport example?
draft_answer: Across the papers, sustainability assessment and evaluation frameworks are consistently presented as multi-criteria, indicator-based tools for comparing alternatives and tracking performance, rather than as single-metric checks [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000] [W3185590208||ABSTRACT||000] [W4377861392||ABSTRACT||000]. In district heating, the assessment is explicitly linked to MCDA, with methods such as WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA used to compare options across criteria, and sensitivity analysis used to judge credibility; the study concludes that all are suitable but differ in calculation and interpretation [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, district heating and related renewable-energy systems are described through social, economic, environmental, technical, and institutional indicator groups, showing that the framework is broad in scope and includes CO2 emission among the environmental indicators [W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001]. In positive energy neighbourhoods, the framework is also tied to integrated design and operational monitoring, covering energy and power performance, GHG emissions, indoor environmental quality, smartness, flexibility, life cycle costs, and social sustainability [W3185590208||ABSTRACT||000]. For public transport, the review found that Multi-Criteria Decision-Making was the preferred framework among 69 references, followed by Assessment Indicator Models, and within MCDM the Analytical Hierarchy Process was the most frequently used approach [W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the provided evidence does not identify a single “most used” method across the district heating studies, since the district heating paper lists several methods but does not rank them [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. Regarding the urban transport example, the available evidence only supports that the environmental side of the framework links to CO2 and GHG emissions reduction, without providing a more detailed causal or quantitative account [W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainability assessment should inform planning, design, and monitoring, but they differ in emphasis: district heating work stresses MCDA comparison, PT work stresses MCDM/AHP preference, and PED-related work stresses indicator completeness and framework integration [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000] [W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001] [W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: District heating sustainability assessment is linked to MCDA, using WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, with sensitivity analysis used to judge credibility [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]

In PT evaluation, Multi-Criteria Decision-Making was the preferred framework among 69 references, and the Analytical Hierarchy Process was the most frequently used MCDM method [W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]

Sustainability frameworks are broad and multi-criteria, covering social, economic, environmental, technical, and institutional indicators in district heating and related systems [W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001]
In the urban transport example, the environmental framework is linked to CO2 and GHG emissions reduction [W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001]
Positive energy neighbourhood frameworks connect assessment and evaluation to integrated design and operational monitoring across multiple performance dimensions [W3185590208||ABSTRACT||000]

limitations_and_uncertainty: The district heating summary does not identify which MCDA method was most used, only that several methods were applied [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

The provided evidence does not directly connect district heating studies with PT evaluation studies in a single shared framework, so the linkage is inferred only at a high level from their common multi-criteria/indicator-based structure [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000] [W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000].
The urban transport CO2-reduction example is only described at a general level; the evidence does not provide detailed outcomes, magnitudes, or causal mechanisms [W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001].

Some papers emphasize framework completeness and integration rather than method frequency, so the cross-paper comparison of ‘most used’ methods is limited to the PT review and cannot be generalized to all studies [W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000] [W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do innovation, CEOs' sustainability orientation, and green governance relate to sustainability and environmental performance in firms?
draft_answer: Across the summaries, innovation consistently appears to be linked to better sustainability or environmental outcomes, but often through mediating organizational mechanisms rather than as a standalone driver. Green innovation is reported to have significant positive relationships with environmental sustainability and innovation climate in industrial firms, with innovation climate mediating this link and green motivational strategies and green abilities strengthening the effect [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||001]. A separate study likewise finds that green innovation capabilities influence firm performance indirectly through social and economic sustainability, although not through environmental sustainability, which suggests the pathway from innovation to performance may differ by sustainability dimension [https://openalex.org/W3200508375||ABSTRACT||001]. In addition, sustainability-oriented innovations are associated with stronger economic performance, with green competitive advantage as a strong mediator and green image as a weak mediator, and they are also positively related to green organizational identity [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000]. On the leadership side, environmentally aware or green transformational leaders are found to positively influence green performance, partly because green organizational culture and green engagement mediate that relationship [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000]. For CEOs and governance, the evidence suggests that governance matters most when considered as a bundle: in dirty firms, CEOs, boards, and owners jointly shape environmental innovation, and both powerful and weak CEOs can support environmental innovation when paired with suitable board and ownership configurations [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]. A broader sustainability-strategy study also reports that genuine sustainability strategy improves firm performance and environmental results, but its effectiveness depends on ownership dispersion and board independence, and the relationship varies by sector [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainability and environmental performance are enhanced by innovation and governance arrangements, but they also show that effects are indirect, contingent, and context-dependent rather than universal [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Green innovation is positively associated with environmental sustainability, and this relationship is mediated by innovation climate in industrial firms [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||001].

Green innovation capabilities affect firm performance indirectly through social and economic sustainability, but not through environmental sustainability [https://openalex.org/W3200508375||ABSTRACT||001].

Green transformational leadership has a positive influence on green performance, with green organizational culture and green engagement acting as mediators [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000].

Environmental innovation depends on governance bundles involving CEOs, boards, and owners, and both powerful and weak CEOs can facilitate it under the right configurations [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000].

Genuinely implemented sustainability strategy improves firm performance and environmental results, but its impact depends on ownership dispersion, board independence, and industry context [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence on CEOs' sustainability orientation is indirect: one paper discusses CEO power and governance bundles, but does not directly measure CEOs' sustainability orientation [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000].

Several studies emphasize mediation and contingent effects, so the relationships are not uniform across firms, sectors, or sustainability dimensions [https://openalex.org/W3200508375||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000].

Some papers explicitly note missing direct evidence on the queried constructs, especially green governance mechanisms and CEOs' sustainability orientation, limiting firm conclusions from those studies alone [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4381617377||ABSTRACT||001].

The governance findings are context-specific, including samples such as dirty firms, Chinese SMEs, industrial firms, and manufacturing-based consumer goods firms, which may limit generalization [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4381617377||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the themes of "energy resources," "clean and distributed energy," and "energy transitions" connect across the context in explaining both environmental sustainability and workforce implications, and what does the context say about the role of clean energy, renewable electricity, and training in this transition?
draft_answer: Across the papers, “energy resources,” “clean and distributed energy,” and “energy transitions” are presented as interconnected parts of a broader shift in how energy systems are organized, governed, and evaluated for sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001]. Several summaries link this shift directly to environmental sustainability, emphasizing reduced greenhouse gas emissions, climate protection, resource conservation, low ecological impacts, and ecosystem stability as core goals [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3154213043||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001]. The context also frames clean and distributed energy through renewable adoption, resilient grids, storage, and a sustainable mix of renewables with limited nonrenewables to maintain supply quality while minimizing cost and environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the transition is not purely technical: it is repeatedly described as involving policy coherence, cross-border collaboration, stakeholder values, and tradeoffs among economic development, ecological standards, inclusivity, and pace of change [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001]. Workforce implications are present in multiple summaries, which tie sustainable energy policies to job creation, economic growth, social equity, human capital development, and public engagement [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001]. One paper makes this especially explicit by saying renewable energy use can support sustained employment growth and that governments should invest in renewable energy infrastructure and workforce training to enable green economic transformation [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the context suggests that clean energy and renewable electricity are treated as central tools for environmental sustainability, but the transition must also be managed as a social and labor-market process requiring training, institutions, and collaboration [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: The papers connect energy resources and energy transitions to environmental sustainability by emphasizing emissions reduction, resource conservation, low ecological impact, and ecosystem stability [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3154213043||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001].

Clean and distributed energy is framed as a renewable-based transition supported by storage, resilient grids, and a sustainable mix of renewables with limited nonrenewables to keep electricity reliable and flexible while lowering environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001].

Workforce implications appear through claims about job creation, economic growth, social equity, human capital development, and workforce training as part of sustainable energy transitions [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001].

Several summaries describe the transition as a policy and governance problem that requires coherence, collaboration, stakeholder inclusion, and balancing economic development with ecological standards [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000].

Renewable energy is described as central to a just and sustainable transition, with one paper explicitly stating that its role in sustainable development is unquestionable and another linking it to sustained employment growth [https://openalex.org/W3175891888||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Not all papers address workforce implications, clean energy, renewable electricity, or training directly, so some connections in the synthesis rely on combining partial evidence across summaries [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3154213043||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence is uneven across contexts and regions, including a Portugal pilot case and a Saudi Arabia policy framework, so the findings may not generalize across all energy transitions [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001].

Some summaries explicitly note missing details, especially on training, renewable electricity, or the specific workforce effects of clean and distributed energy, limiting how precisely those themes can be characterized [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W1557485392||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3175891888||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the themes of "Environmental sustainability", "Sustainability implementation barriers", and "Sustainable residential buildings" connect when comparing off-site construction research with the barrier analysis in Ghana and the "Mostadam" approach in Saudi Arabia, and what sustainability-related findings are highlighted across these contexts?
draft_answer: Across the provided studies, the common thread is that sustainability in construction is treated as an applied, implementation-oriented issue rather than an abstract objective, especially in residential buildings and broader built-environment projects [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. In Ghana, environmental sustainability is operationalized through lifecycle-based project indicators, especially water quality, air quality, energy use and conservation, and environmental compliance and management, which are presented as key measures for steering the industry toward sustainability [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||001]. In the Ghana residential-building barrier study, sustainability implementation barriers are grouped into management, standards, society, and knowledge, with management-related barriers emerging as the most significant obstacle [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001]. This barrier emphasis is consistent with the Ghana retrofit study, which identifies cultural, economic, technical knowledge, and regulatory barriers and argues that overcoming human-behavioral, cost, skills, and policy constraints is important for promoting sustainable retrofitting [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001]. Similar barrier hierarchies appear elsewhere as well: the Nigeria study highlights poor sustainability education, lack of incentives, ignorance of lifecycle cost benefits, low priority for sustainable construction, and resistance to cultural change, while the Iran study finds economics- and regulation-dependent barriers more influential than market or workforce-experience issues [https://openalex.org/W3145060410||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132259306||ABSTRACT||000]. By contrast, the Saudi Arabia “Mostadam” source emphasizes sustainable residential buildings, practical strategies, and policy action to transform buildings and cities toward sustainable development and sustainable cities, but the provided evidence does not specify implementation barriers there [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. The off-site/prefabrication context also fits the same sustainability pattern: the Southern Africa IPCM study mainstreams sustainability principles into affordable housing and reports higher overall sustainability performance using lifecycle energy, cost, and technical-performance evaluation [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000]. Another housing-focused study similarly links environmental sustainability and affordability through passive design, recycled and local materials, and socio-technical innovations that reduce lifecycle costs [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that environmental sustainability, sustainable residential buildings, and sustainability implementation barriers are connected by a shared concern with translating sustainability principles into measurable project indicators, practical housing design, and policy-supported implementation, while the main obstacles are managerial, educational, economic, regulatory, and cultural [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: In Ghana, environmental sustainability is framed through lifecycle-based indicators, especially water quality, air quality, energy use and conservation, and environmental compliance and management [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||001].

The Ghana residential-building study groups sustainability implementation barriers into management, standards, society, and knowledge, and identifies management-related barriers as the most significant obstacle [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How can healthcare workers balanc innovation with sustainability when reducing workplace emissions and avoid the wasteful use of medical resources in imaging and other care, while still keepin AI benefits responsible?
draft_answer: Across the papers, a consistent message is that healthcare workers should treat sustainability as a core design constraint rather than an afterthought when adopting AI and other innovations [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||000]. In radiology and interventional radiology, the literature describes significant environmental burdens from energy use, carbon emissions, waste, water pollution, hardware waste, and data storage, while also noting that awareness of sustainability is often higher than actual implementation [https://openalex.org/W4327898048||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers suggest that AI can still be part of the solution if it is used to reduce low-value imaging, optimize resource allocation, improve workflow efficiency, and support energy efficiency and telemedicine-like sustainable practices [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the same evidence warns that AI can also add sustainability burdens and clinical risks, including algorithmic bias, unequal access, and dangerous recommendations, so benefits should be weighed against equity and patient safety [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||000]. The most repeated prescription is a holistic governance approach: eco-design, lifecycle assessment, responsible data management, continuous monitoring, policy frameworks, and collaboration are all presented as necessary to keep AI benefits responsible [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||001]. More generally, sustainability should be judged through health, justice, and resource conservation, not carbon alone, so workers can avoid wasteful use of medical resources while still improving care [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence also suggests that individual effort is not enough in settings like interventional radiology because some constraints require departmental, institutional, or system-level change [https://openalex.org/W4327898048||ABSTRACT||000]. query: How does the text link economic sustainability and decoupling consumption from economic growth in these two contexts, and what is suggested about making space tourism environmentally sustainable?
draft_answer: Across these summaries, economic sustainability is treated as the most plausible dimension of space tourism sustainability, in the sense that the sector may be financially viable even if broader sustainability remains uncertain [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002]. At the same time, the text says that economic burden persists because of the “tyranny of the rocket equation,” where fuel weight keeps costs and environmental costs tightly linked [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. In this framing, decoupling consumption from economic growth is not presented as already achieved in space tourism; instead, the literature notes that economic indicators are the most relevant while social and environmental indicators are less developed, suggesting that sustainability assessments still emphasize growth-related economic performance more than a fuller decoupling-based model [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014]. The summaries also agree that social and environmental sustainability are less promising than economic sustainability and need a stronger conceptual and empirical basis [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002]. To make space tourism environmentally sustainable, the text suggests first critically evaluating whether it can be made sustainable and ethical at all, and under what preconditions [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. It further recommends developing a theoretically grounded and robust analytical framework adapted from sustainable tourism frameworks to address the current knowledge gap [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. Overall, the evidence implies that environmental sustainability would require more than economic viability; it would require a new framework that can systematically incorporate environmental and social dimensions rather than relying mainly on economic indicators [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002].

key_claims.claim: Space tourism is portrayed as potentially economically sustainable or financially viable, but this does not imply that it is environmentally or socially sustainable [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002].

The summaries suggest that sustainability work in space tourism has focused more on economic indicators than on social and environmental ones, making decoupling from growth unclear in this context [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014].

The text recommends critically examining whether space tourism can be sustainable and ethical at all, and under what preconditions, rather than assuming environmental sustainability is already achievable [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003].

A robust, theoretically grounded analytical framework adapted from sustainable tourism frameworks is proposed as necessary for evaluating space tourism sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The summaries indicate that social and environmental sustainability are less developed, so the evidence base for decoupling consumption from economic growth in space tourism remains weak [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014].

No concrete preconditions or operational measures for making space tourism environmentally sustainable are specified in the summaries beyond developing a new framework and critically evaluating feasibility [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003].

query: How do regional integration and multistakeholder partnerships support Sustainable Development Goal 8 in the Yangtze River Delta?
draft_answer: Evidence specific to the Yangtze River Delta suggests that regional integration supports SDG-related progress by linking sustainability analysis and governance across multiple scales, from county to region, river basin, and global levels [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001]. One study argues that SDG planning should integrate land, water, and energy in long-term urban planning and explicitly include multi-sector partnerships, which it presents as a way to coordinate development across scales and sectors [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001]. Another paper shows that county-level, region-wide sustainability assessment in the YRD can reveal spatial differences and autocorrelations, and that regional sustainability improved overall from 2000 to 2015 even though socio-economic sustainability rose in most counties while environmental sustainability declined [https://openalex.org/W3194996912||ABSTRACT||000]. This indicates that integration is useful not because one dimension can be advanced alone, but because economic and environmental objectives need to be coordinated together [https://openalex.org/W3194996912||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the YRD is described as a useful subnational experimental site for studying regional integration and sustainable development, with calls for applicable governance structures, institutions, multi-source data, and interdisciplinary methods to support integrated development [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001]. Multistakeholder partnerships are also framed in the SDG literature as a way to define scope, identify interlinkages, assign responsibilities, and bring together relevant actors for implementation, while linkages across sectors, scales, and actors help determine who should be engaged [https://openalex.org/W4205386374||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the partnership literature is not uniformly optimistic: reviews report limited effectiveness, legitimacy deficits, and weak synergy generation in many partnerships, suggesting that better governance, accountability, and institutional design are needed [https://openalex.org/W4400486548||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the papers imply that in the YRD, regional integration supports SDG 8 mainly by enabling coordinated, multi-scalar governance of economic development, while multistakeholder partnerships provide the collaborative structure needed to align sectors and actors around that goal [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: Regional integration in the Yangtze River Delta is presented as a way to connect sustainability and development across county, regional, river-basin, and global scales [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers do not discuss SDG 8 directly, so the link to decent work and economic growth in the Yangtze River Delta is often inferential rather than explicit [https://openalex.org/W3194996912||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001].

Some evidence is general to SDGs or to sustainability governance and does not specifically analyze the Yangtze River Delta, so region-specific conclusions remain limited [https://openalex.org/W4400486548||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4205386374||ABSTRACT||000].

The YRD evidence emphasizes assessment and governance frameworks more than measured SDG 8 outcomes, so further research would be needed to show direct effects on employment or economic growth [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001].

However, other evidence suggests the link is often weak in practice: one large study of 8,500 companies found no correlation in reporting specific goals and a clear disconnection between sustainability performance and SDG reporting, implying that firms may disclose SDGs arbitrarily rather than based on actual performance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000]. A related study found that companies may mention SDGs in reports without explaining how concrete sustainability initiatives shape their contribution to the Agenda 2030, reinforcing concerns about transparency and substance [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, some papers report more positive associations, such as a sustainability reporting score index that integrates SDGs and is said to help stakeholders measure firms’ sustainable performance, and another study that links sustainability reporting to sustainability performance through environmental performance measurement and SDG implementation [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001].

From the supply chain perspective, the evidence suggests that sustainability reporting and SDG-related performance become more meaningful when they are embedded in supply chain or value-chain frameworks. A supply-chain assessment framework based on GRI is designed to measure both companies’ and suppliers’ environmental and social sustainability performance using 91 indicators, showing how reporting can extend across supply chain actors and sectors [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper reports that sustainable supply chain management has positive relationships with both SDGs and financial performance, and that implementing a sustainable supply chain from supplier to customer can improve operational efficiency and reduce environmental and social impacts [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001]. Similarly, a framework paper argues that sustainable supply chain management, technology adoption, and performance measurement are important for promoting sustainability, and that clearer sustainability indicators are needed to support SDG-oriented supply chain management [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000].

There is also evidence that SDG alignment in sustainability assessment is not automatic: some indicators have no direct or indirect SDG connection, partly because of limited life-cycle thinking and limited discussion of workers, consumers, and value-chain actors [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001]. Related SDG–LCSA work says SDGs and life-cycle approaches are complementary but lack a harmonized way to connect them, so more research is needed to consistently link metrics to SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers suggest that sustainability reporting can support SDG tracking and sustainability performance measurement, but its credibility and usefulness improve when reports are tied to materiality, performance indicators, and supply-chain-wide assessment rather than broad symbolic disclosure [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Sustainability reporting can be used to show whether SDGs matter to firms and to evaluate sustainability strategy, but this depends on how reporting is designed and implemented [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000].

One large study found no correlation in SDG-specific reporting and a disconnect between sustainability performance and SDG reporting, suggesting reporting can be decoupled from real performance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000].

A supply-chain sustainability assessment framework can measure both companies’ and suppliers’ environmental and social performance across actors and sectors using indicators derived from literature and GRI [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000].

There is no harmonized way yet to connect SDGs and life-cycle assessment metrics, so further research is needed to consistently link these frameworks [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers explicitly note missing or incomplete links between reported SDGs and actual sustainability performance, so the relationship is not consistently evidenced across studies [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000].

Supply chain relevance is unevenly addressed: some papers provide supply-chain frameworks, while others do not mention supply chains at all, limiting direct comparison [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence includes different sectors and approaches, but it does not provide a single harmonized method for linking sustainability reporting, SDGs, and supply-chain performance [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000].

Some findings are descriptive or framework-oriented rather than causal, so the papers do not prove that improved reporting necessarily causes better sustainability or financial outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the circular economy and sustainable recycling approaches in textile waste and polymeric membranes reduce environmental impact?
draft_answer: Across the textile papers, the circular economy is presented as a way to reduce environmental impact by replacing linear production and disposal with reduce-reuse-recycle systems that extend product lifecycles and turn waste into new resources such as recycled yarn, regenerated fibers, biofilms, biodegradable composites, and biofuels [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000]. Multiple reviews agree that recycling, reuse, repair, repurposing, resale, and rental can lower waste and reduce water, resource, and energy use, while also supporting responsible consumption and production [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers also emphasize that designing textiles and finishes for end-of-life recyclability, and using closed-loop or bio-based processing, can help keep materials circulating and reduce pollution from textile production and processing [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature notes that fast fashion-driven overproduction and overconsumption intensify textile waste and environmental pollution, so greener technologies and stricter environmental legislation are needed alongside circular strategies [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000]. For polymeric materials, the plastics review makes a parallel argument: traditional mechanical recycling is insufficient, whereas chemical and biological recycling methods such as pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation are described as more efficient and sustainable alternatives that reduce waste [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the shared environmental logic is that circular and sustainable recycling approaches reduce impact by keeping materials in use longer, limiting virgin resource demand, and decreasing waste generation and pollution [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the papers also caution that recycling is constrained by technological, awareness, and investment barriers, and that existing textile waste management programs have been unsuccessful, so supportive policies, corporate change, and new biotechnologies are needed for these benefits to be realized [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Circular economy textile systems reduce environmental impact by extending product lifecycles and converting waste into reusable outputs such as recycled yarn, regenerated fibers, biofilms, biodegradable composites, and biofuels [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000].

Reuse, repair, recycling, repurposing, resale, and rental are all presented as circular strategies that reduce textile waste and lower water, resource, and energy consumption [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000].

Designing textiles for end-of-life recyclability and using bio-based processing can support closed-loop textile systems and reduce pollution from textile production and processing [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000].

For plastics and polymeric materials, chemical and biological recycling methods such as pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation are described as more sustainable alternatives to traditional mechanical recycling [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000].

The literature also indicates that the environmental benefits of recycling are limited by technological, awareness, and investment barriers, and by unsuccessful existing textile waste management programs [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The supplied evidence is much stronger for textiles than for polymeric membranes, and one summary explicitly notes that no paper-supported membrane recycling summary can be made from the available chunk.
Several papers are reviews or broad conceptual discussions, so they describe intended environmental benefits but provide little quantified evidence of impact reduction.

The literature also flags implementation barriers—especially technology, awareness, investment, and policy constraints—so the promised environmental gains may not be achieved in practice without broader system changes.

query: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?
draft_answer: Across the papers, textile waste management is consistently framed as moving away from dumping and toward recovery, reprocessing, reuse, recycling, and broader circular-economy models [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries show that waste conversion can turn textiles into new products or resource streams, including conversion into purified fiber fractions, recycled fiber products, glucose, bio-oil, and other valuable resources [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. The conversion pathways reported include aggressive mechanical agitation with cellulase-catalyzed hydrolysis, chemical and biotechnological conversion, enzymatic recycling, and fluidized-bed pyrolysis, with pretreatment and solvent recovery noted as important for efficiency and scalability [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the papers agree that textile waste is difficult to process because of mixed fibers, finishes, additives, dyes, and other contaminants that can interfere with degradation and make conversion less efficient [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000]. In contrast, adsorption is discussed mainly in the context of textile wastewater treatment rather than direct conversion of textile materials: it is described as a feasible, cost-effective method for removing dyes and metals, often as part of multi-stage treatment systems [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. Thus, if the goal is to use textile waste management for waste conversion and adsorption-based treatment, the evidence supports a combined strategy in which solid textile wastes are reprocessed into new materials or fuels while liquid effluents are treated with adsorption and other complementary processes [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also suggests that biological treatment, especially using microorganisms and enzymes, may generate valuable new products and clean energy, but the summaries do not provide enough detail to show how these approaches compare directly with adsorption-based methods [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence supports integrating conversion, pretreatment, and adsorption within a circular waste-management framework, but it does not establish a single universal solution for all textile waste streams [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Textile waste management is increasingly framed as a circular system emphasizing recovery, reprocessing, reuse, and recycling rather than dumping [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000].

Textile waste can be converted into valuable outputs through methods such as cellulase-catalyzed hydrolysis, chemical and biotechnological conversion, enzymatic recycling, and pyrolysis [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000].

Pretreatment is important because mixed fibers, dyes, finishes, and additives can interfere with textile waste conversion and degrade efficiency [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000].

Adsorption is presented as a feasible, cost-effective option for removing dyes and metals from textile wastewater, usually alongside other treatment stages [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000].

Biological treatment using microorganisms and enzymes is described as a cleaner textile-waste solution that may generate valuable new products and clean energy [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The summaries do not show that adsorption properties are being used directly in textile solid waste materials; the adsorption evidence is mainly about wastewater treatment.

Some abstracts mention promising conversion yields or energy savings, but the evidence is limited to summary-level statements and does not provide full methodological details or broad comparative analysis.

The papers emphasize that no single universally applicable solution exists for complex textile effluents, so the best combination of conversion and adsorption methods may vary by waste stream [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000].
Several summaries note barriers such as dyes, mixed fibers, and additives, but they do not quantify how these barriers vary across textile types or real-world settings.

query: How is the translational regulation of NEDD4 linked to the IGF1 signaling pathway, and what does the context say about NEDD4 in cells that depend on this pathway?
draft_answer: The clearest evidence linking NEDD4 to the IGF1 pathway comes from gastric cancer cells, where cells were stratified into IGF1R-dependent and IGF1R-independent groups based on Akt phosphorylation after OSI906 treatment [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000]. In that setting, Dox-induced NEDD4 knockdown suppressed tumor growth and NEDD4 overexpression promoted growth specifically in IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells, indicating that NEDD4 supports proliferation in cells that rely on IGF1/IGF1R signaling [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. The study further concludes that NEDD4 promotes proliferation by antagonizing PTEN’s protein phosphatase activity toward IRS1, with a PTEN-IRS1 axis required for NEDD4-mediated regulation of Akt activation and tumor growth [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. In contrast, in IGF1R-independent cells, changing NEDD4 levels had no effect on proliferation, which supports a context-dependent role for NEDD4 rather than a universal growth effect [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. Other provided papers do not add support for an IGF1-NEDD4 translational link: several explicitly state that they do not mention NEDD4 or IGF1 signaling and instead focus on unrelated pathways or proteins [pmc_PMC9803678||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC4425028||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4285014207||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3199735924||ABSTRACT||000]. A related but distinct NEDD4 study in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma shows translational upregulation of NEDD4 and links it to PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling, but it does not explicitly connect NEDD4 to IGF1 [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that NEDD4 can be translationally upregulated in cancer and that, at least in IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells, it promotes growth through a PTEN-IRS1-Akt mechanism, while showing little or no effect in IGF1R-independent cells [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In gastric cancer, NEDD4 was linked to IGF1 signaling by showing stronger growth effects in IGF1R-dependent cells than in IGF1R-independent cells [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].
NEDD4 promotes proliferation in IGF1/IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells through a PTEN-IRS1 axis that regulates Akt activation [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].
In IGF1R-independent gastric cancer cells, NEDD4 silencing or overexpression had no effect on proliferation [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].

A separate pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma study found NEDD4 to be translationally upregulated, but it connected NEDD4 to PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling rather than IGF1 signaling [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Only one provided paper directly addresses NEDD4 in the context of IGF1/IGF1R-dependent cells, so the evidence base is narrow.

The summaries do not provide a detailed mechanistic explanation of how translational regulation specifically controls NEDD4 in the IGF1 context; the strongest support is for functional dependence on IGF1R signaling rather than a direct translation mechanism.

Several papers explicitly do not mention NEDD4 or IGF1 signaling, so they cannot be used to generalize beyond the gastric cancer context [pmc_PMC9803678||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC4425028||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4285014207||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3199735924||ABSTRACT||000].

The pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma study supports translational upregulation of NEDD4 in cancer, but because it does not mention IGF1, it leaves open whether similar translational control operates in IGF1-dependent cells [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
draft_answer: In the EU context, the SDGs are repeatedly presented as a framework for policy coherence for sustainable development, because they are meant to integrate environmental, social, and economic objectives and prevent progress in one area from undermining another [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers treat coherence as a practical alignment task: for example, the SDGs are linked to the European Green Deal, the European Semester, and Country-Specific Recommendations through a 3D-mapping approach meant to better align EU priorities with the broader sustainability agenda [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. Other work suggests that tools such as circular economy policy and Life Cycle Assessment can support this alignment by connecting EU policy design and monitoring to SDG achievement [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence is not uniformly optimistic: one paper argues that SDG-linked coherence can become narrowly technical, mask political incoherencies, and even limit transformative change when framed as “neutral” or “win-win” [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper similarly stresses that coherence depends on political drivers—ideas, interests, and institutions—rather than being only an administrative or institutional exercise [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the EU literature, the environmental SDGs appear to be the most complex and least coherent, implying that coherence is weakest in environmental policy areas and especially needs strengthening around biodiversity and climate [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. Relatedly, one study says the SDGs are already incorporated into EU strategic priorities to a sufficient extent, but important sustainability challenges identified in the Sustainable Development Report 2020 are still not reflected in the CSRs, showing that coherence remains incomplete [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. More broadly, the literature calls for a system perspective, better data, and more transdisciplinary research to capture trade-offs and improve coherence across governance levels and scales of implementation [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: In the EU context, the SDGs are used as a framework for policy coherence for sustainable development because they integrate environmental, social, and economic objectives and are meant to avoid progress in one area undermining another [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

EU policy coherence is operationalized through alignment efforts such as mapping SDGs with the European Green Deal and the European Semester’s Country-Specific Recommendations [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001].

Circular economy strategy and Life Cycle Assessment are presented as instruments that can strengthen EU policy coherence with the SDGs by supporting policy design, monitoring, and cross-framework alignment [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000].

The environmental SDGs are described as the most complex and least coherent in the EU analysis, suggesting that coherence is weakest in environmental areas, especially biodiversity and climate [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

One paper warns that SDG-based policy coherence can be narrowed into technical solutions that obscure political incoherencies and may limit transformative change if treated as neutral or purely win-win [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000].

The literature calls for a system perspective, better data availability, and more transdisciplinary research to improve coherence across governance levels, scales, and trade-offs [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The summaries indicate multiple approaches to policy coherence, but they do not provide comparable empirical results across all EU member states or policy sectors, so the overall strength of coherence across the EU remains uncertain.

Several papers emphasize conceptual frameworks or mapping exercises rather than outcome evidence, so it is unclear how much these coherence tools have actually changed policy or sustainability performance in practice.
The evidence points especially to environmental SDGs as weakly coherent, but the summaries do not show whether similar weaknesses exist for all other goal areas in the same way.
One paper focuses on the Dutch case and another on broader EU-level strategy, so some findings may not generalize uniformly across the EU.

query: How are Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) and optimization used in sustainability evaluation frameworks for transport systems, and what methods are highlighted for road transport sustainability analysis?
draft_answer: Across the papers, sustainability evaluation for transport systems is consistently framed as a multi-criteria decision-making problem because transportation decisions involve multiple, often conflicting criteria that must be balanced under uncertainty [https://openalex.org/W4320918985||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies emphasize that MCDM/MCDA is used to combine environmental, economic, social, and sometimes circularity dimensions into a single evaluative framework or index, supporting more reliable decision-making than simpler sustainability indices alone [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000]. In transport applications, one paper proposes an integrated spherical fuzzy set approach with SWARA for weighting and MARCOS for ranking sustainable vehicles in Tehran, while another uses an entropy–CoCoSo framework to evaluate road transportation sustainability in OECD countries [https://openalex.org/W4320918985||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000]. A broader transport case study also uses hybrid MCDM methods—DEMATEL, REMBRANDT, and VIKOR—and compares them with AHP, Fuzzy AHP, TOPSIS, and PROMETHEE in expressway location evaluation, showing that multiple MCDA tools are used in sustainability assessment workflows [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000]. For public transport, the literature review finds MCDM to be the preferred framework type among surveyed studies, and identifies AHP as the most frequently used method, while another public transport framework combines indicators into the Sustainable Transport Planning Index using AHP-based weights and normalization [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4363679553||ABSTRACT||000]. Optimization is mentioned more as a general decision-support goal than as a specific transport-method family in the provided evidence, and one review explicitly does not support naming optimization frameworks beyond MCDA-based approaches [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4378909343||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that transport sustainability frameworks favor structured multi-criteria ranking, weighting, and normalization methods, with entropy, AHP, SWARA, MARCOS, CoCoSo, VIKOR, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, DEMATEL, and REMBRANDT highlighted across the studies [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4363679553||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Transport sustainability evaluation is repeatedly treated as an MCDM/MCDA problem because it involves multiple conflicting criteria and decision uncertainty [https://openalex.org/W4320918985||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000].

Road transport sustainability analysis is explicitly framed with an entropy–CoCoSo framework, where entropy provides objective criterion weights and CoCoSo performs ranking [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000].

A road transport case study uses hybrid MCDM methods including DEMATEL, REMBRANDT, and VIKOR, and compares them with AHP, Fuzzy AHP, TOPSIS, and PROMETHEE [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000].

In public transport sustainability literature, MCDM is the preferred framework type among the reviewed references, and AHP is the most frequently used method [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000].

Some sustainability frameworks combine indicators into a single index using MCDM, such as the Sustainable Transport Planning Index, which uses AHP-based weights, normalization, and a weighted average [https://openalex.org/W4363679553||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The provided evidence is uneven across transport modes: road transport methods are described in detail for only a few studies, while other papers are broader MCDA reviews or public-transport-focused frameworks.

Optimization is not consistently specified as a distinct methodological family in the summaries, so the evidence supports MCDM/MCDA strongly but only limited direct claims about optimization methods in transport sustainability evaluation.
Several papers are reviews or framework papers rather than empirical comparisons, so the evidence does not establish that any one method is universally best for transport sustainability assessment.
Some summaries explicitly note that transport-specific or road-specific methods are not identified in the excerpted evidence, limiting how far the synthesis can go beyond the named methods.

query: How do the methods described for road transport sustainability and sustainable urban transport contribute to sustainable transportation systems, and what role do simulation, optimization, machine learning, and fuzzy sets play in designing and operating such systems?
draft_answer: Across these papers, sustainable transportation systems are consistently framed as requiring more than cost and service efficiency: they must also account for environmental, social, and often economic impacts in both metropolitan and broader transport contexts [W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000][W4386954171||ABSTRACT||002][W4388202057||ABSTRACT||000]. The road-transport and urban-transport literature therefore contributes to sustainability by supporting better planning, policy-making, and operational decisions that reduce externalities such as emissions, congestion, and other undesirable effects [W3160296158||ABSTRACT||000][W4380272563||ABSTRACT||001][W3142667272||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers emphasize that integrated planning instruments and management approaches, including Sustainable Urban Mobility Plans and Intelligent Transport Systems, help cities shift away from traditional transport planning toward sustainability-oriented strategy and implementation [W3142667272||ABSTRACT||000]. In this synthesis, simulation, optimization, machine learning, and fuzzy sets appear as core methodological tools for designing and efficiently operating sustainable transportation systems, because they are reviewed as methods that support system design, operation, and future research development [W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000]. The evidence also suggests a model-based decision-making pattern in which predictive models, MADM methods, and quantitative models help planners evaluate interventions such as fare reductions, traffic-flow optimization, and emissions reduction [W4380272563||ABSTRACT||001][W4388440263||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, literature reviews and assessment-focused studies indicate that sustainable transport research still has gaps, including ambiguous assignment of criteria to sustainability dimensions and limited analysis of some mode combinations and variables [W3177488261||ABSTRACT||001][W3160296158||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, sustainable urban transport research is not limited to technical methods alone; it also includes new vehicle technologies, GIS, time-series analyses, electrification, and innovative sharing-mobility business models, while behavioral aspects receive less attention [W4366773389||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainability-oriented transport systems are built through coordinated planning, evidence-based evaluation, and methodological tools that improve both design and operation, but they differ in how specifically they document those tools and in the extent to which they address behavioral and multi-modal complexity [W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000][W3142667272||ABSTRACT||000][W4386954171||ABSTRACT||002].

key_claims.claim: Sustainable transportation systems are defined by attention to environmental, social, and economic impacts, not only monetary cost and service quality [W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000][W4386954171||ABSTRACT||002][W4388202057||ABSTRACT||000]

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers explicitly note insufficient evidence for specific methodological roles, so the precise contributions of simulation, optimization, machine learning, and fuzzy sets are only clearly stated in one review and not in all papers [W4366773389||ABSTRACT||001][W3142667272||ABSTRACT||000][W3177488261||ABSTRACT||001].

The evidence is mostly review- and abstract-level summary, so it provides broad methodological themes rather than detailed comparative performance results or causal effectiveness estimates [W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000][W3126404096||ABSTRACT||001].

Some studies highlight unresolved gaps such as ambiguous sustainability criteria and limited analysis of non-motorized and motorized modes together, indicating that the literature is not yet comprehensive [W3177488261||ABSTRACT||001][W3160296158||ABSTRACT||000].

Overall, the evidence suggests ARDL was applied as a time-series tool to test nexus relationships after stationarity checks, and the only directly supported long-run finding here is that human capital and renewable energy were linked positively with SDGs and negatively with carbon emissions in the China study [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the context of Sustainable Consumption, what did the systematic review conclude about the concept’s complexity, its relationship to the circular economy, and the role of government in supporting sustainable consumption?

The review also suggests that circular economy thinking should move beyond resource efficiency to include broader socio-ecological cycles and the social, political, and ecological implications that technocentric approaches can neglect [https://openalex.org/W4378216524||ABSTRACT||000]. Government is presented as an important enabler of sustainable consumption through its importance, role, and tools, and as a source of policy guidance and public support needed to avoid missed opportunities in sustainable economic growth and environmental stewardship [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4289130621||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the synthesis suggests that sustainable consumption depends on coordinated action across consumers, policy, and broader circular-economy transitions rather than on individual behavior alone [https://openalex.org/W4322770358||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4409544928||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What clinical and laboratory findings are associated with elevated FSH in men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, and how do KS and testicular XX DSD compare with the undefined cause group?
draft_answer: Across the provided studies, elevated serum FSH in men with non-obstructive azoospermia is linked to less favorable reproductive and testicular profiles, including failed sperm retrieval, higher LH, and lower likelihood of successful sperm extraction, whereas successful retrieval is associated with larger testicular volume and a higher T/LH ratio [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||001]. In men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, the Klinefelter syndrome (KS) group had lower average testicular volume, shorter penile length, lower total testosterone, greater height and arm span, higher serum LH and FSH, and more frequent gynecomastia than the undefined-cause group, with gynecomastia absent in the undefined group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. Testicular XX DSD showed an intermediate pattern, with LH, FSH, and penile length values between KS and the undefined-cause group, testicular volume similar to KS, and other clinical data similar to the undefined group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. The comparison therefore suggests that KS is the most distinct from undefined cause, while testicular XX DSD occupies a middle phenotype rather than matching either group completely [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. One additional chromosomal-anomaly cohort reported that certain abnormalities should be referred for AZF deletion screening and that only 1% of cases with >1×10^6 sperm/mL had Y chromosome microdeletions, but it did not provide the specific clinical or laboratory associations requested here [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence supports elevated FSH as part of a broader endocrine/testicular pattern associated with more severe reproductive impairment, but direct cross-study comparisons are limited because not all papers report the same subgroups or outcomes [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001].

Among men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, the KS group has higher serum LH and FSH, lower average testicular volume, shorter penile length, lower total testosterone, and more frequent gynecomastia than the undefined-cause group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001].
